# reorion2

A from-scratch, functionally faithful **native Windows port of Master of Orion II** (MicroProse / SimTex, 1996), rebuilt from a decompilation of the original DOS binary into readable modern C++ / SDL3.

> **Status: work in progress.** The engine boots through the intro and menus, starts a game, and renders the main in-game screens — five of the six of them within 0.15 % of the original, pixel for pixel. Gameplay beyond rendering (turns, combat, diplomacy) is not verified yet. See [Current status](#current-status) below.

## What this is

`Orion2.exe` was decompiled into ~5,100 functions across ~300,000 lines of low-level, DOS-real-mode-flavored C (`sub_XXXXXX` names, raw segment math, `int`-as-pointer tricks, BIOS/DOS interrupt calls). This project incrementally turns that dump into a real, compilable, cross-platform-minded engine:

- BIOS/DOS/VGA/mouse/sound dependencies are extracted into a small `src/port/` layer (inspired by [DOSBox-X](https://github.com/joncampbell123/dosbox-x) and the `remc2` project), built on **SDL3**.
- Memory management moves off segment:offset DOS tricks onto `malloc`/`new`.
- Decompiler artifacts (`JUMPOUT`, `__usercall`, fused/lost register arguments, "possibly undefined" locals, mis-sized buffers) are identified, verified against the original disassembly, and fixed function by function.
- Where an `int` turns out to actually be a pointer, it gets a real type — and a real `struct` when the layout is clear.

The goal is a modern, readable, maintainable codebase that plays identically to the original — not a rewrite, a **faithful, verified translation**.

## Current status

_Last updated: 2026-09-08_

The port is compared against the original running under DOSBox-X, frame by frame,
from the same starting position. Each in-game screen is measured as "how many of
the 307,200 pixels differ":

| Screen | Differing pixels | |
|---|---:|---|
| RACES | **0** | 0.00 % — pixel-identical |
| PLANETS | 8 | 0.00 % |
| FLEETS | 266 | 0.09 % |
| INFO | 321 | 0.10 % |
| COLONIES | 459 | 0.15 % |
| LEADERS | 6,459 | 2.10 % — system view still missing |
| Fleet panel (galaxy map) | 35 | 0.09 % of the panel area — 34 of them one animated background sprite caught mid-phase |

A 600-frame regression harness (`compare_frames`) runs the boot sequence against
recorded DOSBox-X output and currently reports 600/600 identical frames; it has to
stay green for any change to be accepted.

Day-to-day work happens on the **x64 Debug** build, which is what the numbers above
were measured on. x86 still builds, but has not been re-verified against the harness
recently — the fixes are platform-independent, the verification effort simply goes
into one configuration.

Recent milestones (see [`PROGRESS.md`](PROGRESS.md) for the full, wave-by-wave engineering log):

- The intro, menus and game start-up run through; the in-game screens render.
- **Clicking a fleet on the galaxy map now opens a panel that matches the original.**
  It went from "nothing happens" through a crash and a panel drawn 128 px too high
  to a pixel comparison of 35 differing pixels out of 38,016 (0.09 %) — 34 of which
  are an animated background sprite caught at a different phase, leaving one real
  stray pixel. Five waves (161–165), each a different class of decompiler damage;
  the details are in [`PROGRESS.md`](PROGRESS.md).
- Several recurring classes of decompiler damage were identified and are now hunted
  systematically rather than one at a time:
  - **Truncated tables** — a contiguous array in the binary split into a one-element
    symbol plus "the rest", so `table[2*i]` read out of bounds.
  - **Overlapping views** — one record table exposed as several symbols at different
    offsets, all but one of them one element long. Spotted by the *stride* in the
    code: `dword[3*i]`, `word[6*i]`, `byte[12*i]` all mean the same 12-byte record.
  - **Empty thunks** — `push <flag> / jmp <shared body>` decompiled to `JUMPOUT`,
    which is a no-op in the port, so the function silently did nothing.
  - **Dropped return values and lost register arguments** — the Watcom register
    calling convention (`eax/edx/ebx/ecx`) is invisible to the decompiler, so calls
    lost arguments and callers read uninitialized locals instead of results.
  - **The same address under two names** — a stub in `link_stubs.c` and real data in
    `orion_data.c` became two separate objects: one got filled, the other got read.
  - **Silent 32 → 16 bit narrowing** — the original keeps a value in a 16-bit stack
    slot and the callee narrows on entry (`cwde`, or reloading a saved argument
    with `movsx ..., word ptr [ebp+var_N]`). Hex-Rays folds that away, so the port
    passed 32 bits whose upper half was never initialised. A scan of the listing
    found 25 functions of the `cwde` shape — not one of them narrowed.
  - **Shared tails mistaken for no-ops** — a `JUMPOUT` whose target sits just above
    a function epilogue is not necessarily dead: it can be 40 bytes of drawing code
    that two sibling functions share.
- Tooling added alongside the fixes, under `tools/compare/`: byte-level reads from the
  original image (`dumpdata.py`), best-frame matching between port and DOSBox
  (`bestmatch.py`), and scanners for the two aliasing/sizing bug classes
  (`scan_alias.py`, `scan_velikosti.py`). The port itself grew a hardware watchpoint
  (`PortDebug_WatchWrite`, x86 debug registers) that names the exact instruction
  corrupting a global — it found a memory-overwrite bug on the first attempt.
- Known open issues right now: the LEADERS screen draws the correct star system's name
  and map position but leaves the system view itself empty, and a family of string
  helpers (`sub_24ACA` and its thunks) that substitutes numbers into text from the
  game's string archives is still unimplemented, so a few numbers are missing from
  otherwise correct labels.

## Screenshots

Progress screenshots live on the [`wiki`](https://github.com/turican0/reorion2/tree/wiki/screenshots) branch (kept separate so binary images don't bloat `main`'s history).

**2026-08-29 — in-game screens render 1:1 with the original.** Port on the left, original under DOSBox-X on the right, same starting position:

![COLONIES screen, port next to the original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/turican0/reorion2/wiki/screenshots/2026-08-29-colonies-port-vs-original.png)

459 of 307,200 pixels differ (0.15 %) — a single 17×27 rectangle, the scrollbar
thumb, which the original still shades and the port does not.

**2026-08-29 — RACES, from the port alone:**

![RACES screen rendered by the port](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/turican0/reorion2/wiki/screenshots/2026-08-29-races-port.png)

This one is pixel-identical to the original, so a side-by-side would just be the
same image twice.

**2026-07-24 — intro cinematics render correctly:**

![SimTex logo rendering during the intro](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/turican0/reorion2/wiki/screenshots/2026-07-24-intro-simtex-logo.png)

The SimTex logo (first frame of the intro sequence) drawing correctly on real hardware/window — confirms the font/palette/framebuffer fixes from this wave are visually correct, not just crash-free.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph decompiled["src/game/ — decompiled game logic"]
        orion["orion_part_01..26.c\norion_data.c\n(~5,100 functions, being cleaned up incrementally)"]
        compat["decomp_compat.h\n(shims for __fastcall, JUMPOUT, etc.)"]
    end

    subgraph port["src/port/ — modern platform layer"]
        vga["port_vga\nSDL3 framebuffer, palette"]
        sound["port_sound\n(not wired up yet)"]
        mouse["port_mouse"]
        dos["port_dos\nterminal emu, int386 stubs"]
        file["port_file"]
        mem["port_memory\nmalloc/new-based allocator"]
    end

    entry["src/reorion2.cpp\nmain() — inits port layer,\nthen calls GameMain_10057"]

    entry --> port
    entry --> orion
    orion --> port
    orion -.-> compat
```

```
reorion2/
  src/
    reorion2.cpp          # entry point: inits the port layer, then calls GameMain_10057
    game/                 # the decompiled game itself, being incrementally cleaned up
      orion_part_01.c ... orion_part_26.c
      orion_data.c         # global data/tables extracted from the original binary
      decomp_compat.h        # compatibility shims for decompiler artifacts
      orion_common.h        # shared declarations
    port/                 # modern platform layer replacing BIOS/DOS/VGA/mouse/sound
      port_vga.*    port_sound.*   port_mouse.*
      port_dos.*    port_file.*    port_memory.*
  Debug/, x64/Debug/      # build output + game data files (LBX archives) live here
  ref/                    # reference material pulled from the original disassembly
  PROGRESS.md             # detailed, chronological engineering log ("waves")
  prompt.md               # the porting methodology/rules this project follows
```

## Building

Requires Visual Studio 2022 (MSBuild) and the original game's data files (LBX archives) — this repository does not include or distribute them; you need a legally owned copy of Master of Orion II.

```bash
# x86 (Win32)
MSBuild reorion2.sln -p:Configuration=Debug -p:Platform=x86

# x64
MSBuild reorion2.sln -p:Configuration=Debug -p:Platform=x64
```

The game's data files (`*.LBX` and friends) need to sit next to the built executable — `Debug\` for x86, `x64\Debug\` for x64.

```bash
cd Debug && ./reorion2.exe            # x86
cd x64/Debug && ./reorion2.exe        # x64
```

Useful environment variables while debugging:

- `REORION2_TRACE=1` — print diagnostic checkpoints to stderr as the game boots.
- `REORION2_SKIPINTRO=1` — skip the intro cinematics and jump straight to menu init (faster iteration while bisecting crashes).
- `REORION2_SENDKEY=<code>:<ms>` and `REORION2_CLICK="x,y@ms:hold;..."` — scripted input, so a run can drive itself to a specific screen unattended.
- `REORION2_DUMP_DIR=<dir>` with `REORION2_DUMP_AFTER_MS` / `REORION2_DUMP_FRAME_RANGE` — dump raw framebuffers (palette + 640×480 indices) for comparison against DOSBox-X.
- `REORION2_WATCHDOG=<seconds>` — if no frame is presented for that long, suspend the main thread and print its stack. Turns "the window stopped responding" into a call stack.
- `REORION2_PROBE_LOG=1` with `REORION2_PROBE_AFTER_MS` — buffered, timestamped log for temporary probes placed in game code (`PortDebug_ProbeLog`). The threshold matters: drawing functions are called tens of thousands of times before the interesting screen is reached.

## Porting methodology

This project follows a deliberate, verify-before-you-fix process (full rules in [`prompt.md`](prompt.md)):

1. Convert decompiled functions to readable code incrementally, one call graph at a time, starting from `GameMain_10057` (originally `main__0`).
2. Extract real `struct`s instead of raw offset casts (`*(int*)(a1+34)`) wherever the layout is clear.
3. When an `int` turns out to be a pointer, retype it — and pull out a struct once the shape is known.
4. Remove `JUMPOUT`/`goto` artifacts where possible, without changing behavior.
5. Route anything BIOS/DOS/hardware-shaped into `src/port/*.cpp`.
6. Strip decompiler calling-convention noise (`__fastcall`, `__usercall`, ...) once it's confirmed dead.
7. **Always cross-check against the original disassembly** when decompiled control flow, argument counts, or return values look suspicious — the decompiler gets things wrong often enough that "looks weird" is a real signal, not noise. The reference dump (`Orion2.exe` plus its IDA listings) is kept **outside the working tree** — by default `C:/prenos/reorion2Data/diss/`, overridable with `REORION2_DISS`; `tools/compare/diss.py` resolves it. It used to live in `Debug/diss/`, which is gitignored and therefore got wiped on a branch switch.
8. English for all comments and all `.md` documentation.

## Contributing / history

Development log with full technical detail (root causes, asm cross-references, before/after) lives in [`PROGRESS.md`](PROGRESS.md). It's organized into numbered "waves," each one a focused investigation-and-fix session.

## Legal

This repository contains **no original game assets or data files**. It is a clean-room-adjacent engineering exercise built from a decompilation of the executable's *code*, intended for use only with a legally owned copy of Master of Orion II. Master of Orion II is a trademark of its respective rights holders; this is an unofficial, non-commercial fan project.

harrison3000-terep2vb-readme-md.text:
# terep2 in C++

> **This is vibe-coded.** The code and these docs were written by an AI (Claude), steered and
> reviewed by the repository's author, not written line by line by hand. It is checked
> against the original program frame by frame (see [Verification](#verification)), but read it
> with that in mind.

A readable C++ rewrite ("C with classes" style) of **Terep2** (Nagymáthé Dénes, 1996–97,
"-DEFORMERS- Atomic Vehicle Simulation System"), made from the disassembly in
`terep2isolado/reasm/maincode.asm` and the Win16 version. Its behaviour is identical to the
original frame by frame: the framebuffer and the game state match the original asm byte for byte
(see [Verification](#verification)). The exceptions are a bug fixed on purpose (the jump bug
that corrupts the title) and a crash of the original that the port does not reproduce (see
[Things found along the way](#things-found-along-the-way)).

## Building and running

```sh
git submodule update --init   # Dear ImGui and Nuked-OPL3 (host/imgui, host/Nuked-OPL3), for terep2vb
make            # terep2-headless: test host, no dependencies
make sdl        # terep2vb: playable SDL2 + OpenGL 3.3 version (needs libsdl2-dev, OpenGL and the submodules)
make test       # replays the Win16 recordings in tests/ and compares the frames
make -j8 all sdl  # in parallel: each source is its own object in build/, rebuilt when its headers change
make coverage  # which lines of src/ the tests run (clang/LLVM): summary, and build/cov/html
make coverage REPLAY="rec/dir data/Map"  # the same for one recording only
make wasm-test  # the test host built for WebAssembly (wasm32-wasip1: clang + wasi-libc/libc++, no Emscripten), replays run with node
./terep2vb                 # opens the map chooser where the last map was chosen
./terep2vb data/Asphalt    # opens it with that map selected
```

C++17 with GNU extensions (`__attribute__((packed))` for the PCX header, `-fwrapv` and `#embed`), so it builds with
g++ 15+ or clang++ 19+. Tested on Linux x86-64 with both. The code does not depend on pointer
size, but it has not been tested on 32 bits. Physics runs at 120 Hz and the display at 60 Hz, as
in the Win16 port. The game's window opens at the size of the picture at the chosen scale,
enlarged to at least 960x600 and reduced by a whole factor if it does not fit on the screen.
Esc pauses the game and opens a small menu: the render scale (the
window follows it) and the minimap. Esc again resumes; the menu's button goes back to the
chooser, where another map (or other options) can be picked. Each game starts from scratch: `game_init` resets
the global state (`state_reset`) and everything the game allocated (`game_free`).

Window: the SDL host owns one OpenGL 3.3 core context (`host/gui.cpp`). The map chooser, the
game's picture (the software renderer's frame, as a texture, scaled to the window keeping its
shape) and the minimap all go through Dear ImGui on it. The SDL host draws only the game's own
picture; the OpenGL renderer is the web page's (below).

Sound: the game writes the AdLib (OPL2) registers as the original did to ports 388h/389h
(`src/sound.cpp`: an engine voice per view and the crash effect); the SDL host plays them through
[Nuked-OPL3](https://github.com/nukeykt/Nuked-OPL3) (LGPL 2.1, a git submodule), an emulator of
the OPL3 chip that starts in OPL2 mode, from an SDL audio callback at 48 kHz
(`host/opl_sound.cpp`). "Disable sound" in the map chooser leaves the
audio device and the emulator alone. The test host does not play anything.

Minimap ("Minimap" in the map chooser or the Esc menu, off by default): the SDL host draws
the map semi-transparent in the bottom right corner, each cell in its colour and darker where it
is low, with a square in a colour of its own and the number of each car (in the game's font) where
its reference point is; x is to the right and y down, so a camera turned to yaw 0 looks up the
minimap. It is drawn over the game's picture through ImGui (`host/minimap.cpp`), so the
game's picture and the tests do not change.

`terep2vb` opens a map chooser (Dear ImGui): the directories on the left, starting where
the last map was chosen, or at the map directory given on the command line (its only argument),
with that map selected (`[map]` marks those with a `map.pcx` and a
`col.pcx`); on the right a preview of the selected map, its terrain turning, drawn with the
Comanche "voxel space" technique from `map.pcx` (heights) and `col.pcx` (colour of each cell
through its palette); below it the render scale and the options (the first time, the scale
is 3 and `fix-ice-bug` is ticked). A click selects a directory, a double click enters it or
plays the map, like the Play button (which needs a `car1.dat` too). The chooser
lives in `host/` (`launcher.cpp`, `voxel_preview.cpp`, reading the PCX files with `common/pcx`) and
does not touch the game code.

The chooser's choices (scale, minimap, sound, extra options and the last map) are
kept in `prefs.txt`, one `key: value` per line, in SDL's preference directory
(`~/.local/share/terep2vb` on Linux, `%APPDATA%\terep2vb` on Windows). They are read when the
chooser opens and written when a game starts, only if something changed.

Extra options are fixes of bugs of the original, or other changes to what it does; without
them the game behaves like the original (the test host turns them on with `-E name`,
repeatable, `all` for every one). The options are listed in `extra_option_list` (`game.cpp`)
and kept in `extra_options`, which the map chooser shows as checkboxes:

| Name | What it does |
|---|---|
| `fix-ice-bug` | broken ice no longer wraps around to the highest terrain (see below) |
| `hide-banner` | hides the "GAMBIARRA FOREVER!" line that the Win16 port draws at the bottom |

### In a web page

`make web` builds the game as WebAssembly (`web/terep2.wasm`, about 300 KB: clang for
wasm32-wasip1 with the WASI libc and libc++, no Emscripten) with its own small host,
`host_web/web_main.cpp`. The page (`web/index.html`, `web/terep2.js`: `web/` is only what is served) asks for a folder, finds the maps
in it and reads their files right there in the browser (nothing is uploaded), then runs the game
on a canvas with the keyboard, physics at 120 Hz and the picture at 60 Hz as in the SDL host. The
page needs to be served, not opened as a file:

    make web && python3 -m http.server -d web

and then http://localhost:8000. The sound is the same AdLib emulation (Nuked-OPL3, in the module
too, played through an AudioWorklet), and there is the same minimap, in the bottom right corner
of the window. Both renderers: the software one, and the OpenGL one, drawn with WebGL 2:
`host_web/gl_renderer.cpp` (the game's side) and `host_web/rz`, the renderer itself (from Harrison's
[renderizeitor](https://github.com/harrison3000/renderizeitor): PCX files from memory, the page's
canvas), whose WebGL calls are imports of the module done one for one by `web/webgl.js`; its GLSL
ES 3.00 shaders are in `web/shaders.js`, asked for by name. The page draws the text over it; the
draw distance (where the fog starts, 1 to 110 tiles) is a slider by the map list, and the quality
another: high (three shadow cascades of 2048), medium (one of 2048 up to 25 tiles, 0.75 of the
screen's resolution; the default on a touch screen) or low (one of 512 up to 20 tiles, half the
resolution). No map preview; Esc goes back to the list of maps. `make wasm-test` checks the game itself on 32-bit WebAssembly:
the replays give the same frames as the Win16 port there too.

### Higher resolution

The render scale N (the chooser, the Esc menu; `-s N` in the test host) renders at 320·N x 200·N. Scale 1 is the original, byte for byte. At
larger scales only the drawing changes; the game state is identical at any scale:

- the screen, the clipping and the scanline tables grow with it (`render_scale`, `screen_w()`,
  `screen_h()`);
- projection uses the full 16.16 position, relative to the eye, instead of the original's
  whole units (`view_transform_fine` in `scene.cpp`). With whole units a car close to the camera
  jumps several pixels at a time, which at 4x becomes a very visible jitter. Integer camera
  space is still used for the near plane and the facing tests;
- text, sprites, wheels and the pixels of the car model scale by the same factor.

The rest (affine texturing, Gouraud, dithering) is the original rasteriser, just finer.
![`docs/alta_resolucao.gif`](docs/alta_resolucao.gif)
Compares 1x upscaled and 4x.

### Controls

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| arrows + keypad 5 | car 1 (accelerate, brake, left, right, handbrake) |
| W Z A D S | car 2 |
| I M J L K | car 3 |
| T V F H G | car 4 |
| keypad 7 9 1 3 . | car 5 |
| 1 / 2 | "jump" of the car in view 1 / view 2 |
| F1–F5 | camera: on the car, on the car smoothed, fixed, chase, all cars |
| F6 | cycles the camera of view 2 |
| F9 | split screen |
| F10 | near/far fog |
| Tab / Q | switches the car followed by view 1 / view 2 |
| [ ] | increases / decreases gravity |
| + − / * (keypad) | height and distance of the chase camera |

## Layout

```
src/            the game (no OS or library dependencies)
  terep.hpp     value types (Vec3, Coord, Pos), structures (Car, CarVertex, CarSpring,
                Particle, ChaseCam, ProjVertex, PcxHeader...) and prototypes
  fixed.hpp     fixed point: Angle (0x10000 = 360°), Q15 (sine/cosine, matrices), multiplications
  state.cpp     the global state (world, camera, render, map_tables, contact) and its initial values
  font.pbm      the font (plain PBM, 5x5 glyphs one below the other), embedded with #embed
  math.cpp      table-driven sine/cosine, atan2, vector length, rotation matrix
  terrain.cpp   terrain height (2 triangles per heightmap cell)
  physics.cpp   soft body (Car methods): controls, wheels, springs, integration, collision, particles
  camera.cpp    the 5 cameras
  raster.cpp    polygon clipping, near plane, flat/Gouraud/textured filling
  scene.cpp     visible area, terrain with the painter's algorithm, sprites and particles
  car_draw.cpp  car vertex transform and the model interpreter (bytecode)
  text.cpp      bitmap font
  sound.cpp     AdLib registers (the host decides what to do with them)
  car_file.cpp  the carN.dat format: car_read
  load.cpp      the map's PCX layers into the segments, fog/translucency tables, cars, game_init
  game.cpp      one frame (views, text, keys) and the keyboard
host/
  host.hpp      what the hosts share
  common.cpp    starting and freeing a game, time step, case-insensitive file opening
  sdl_main.cpp  SDL2 host
  gui.cpp       its window: one OpenGL 3.3 core context, with ImGui (OpenGL3 backend) on it
  renderer_sw.cpp the game's picture, as a texture scaled to the window
  launcher.cpp  map chooser (Dear ImGui) shown when no map is given
  prefs.cpp     the chooser's preferences file (prefs.txt, "key: value" per line)
  voxel_preview.cpp  the chooser's preview: the map's terrain in voxel space
  opl_sound.cpp the game's AdLib writes played through Nuked-OPL3 and SDL audio
  minimap.cpp   the optional minimap drawn over the game's picture
  imgui/        Dear ImGui (git submodule)
  Nuked-OPL3/   OPL3 emulator (git submodule, LGPL 2.1)
common/
  pcx.cpp       the PCX reader (8 bits, one plane): the game, the chooser's preview and the
                web's renderer
host_web/       the web host (WebAssembly): web_main.cpp, and the OpenGL renderer with WebGL 2,
                gl_renderer.cpp and rz/ (the renderer)
web/            the web page, what is served: index.html, terep2.js, webgl.js, shaders.js,
                opl_player.js and, once built, terep2.wasm
host_test/      the test host (terep2-headless)
  main.cpp      replays a recording of the Win16 port and compares the frames
data/           the maps (not in the repository)
tests/          run_tests.sh and the Win16 recordings (one directory each: record.txt, frames)
tools/          synthetic and face car makers (test maps)
```

### C++ style

C++ only where it makes the code clearer; the rest stays in the classic style (free functions,
`printf`, `memcpy`; from the standard library only `std::swap` and `std::vector` (in the cars);
no exceptions, no inheritance):

- **Value types for fixed point.** `Vec3` (signed 16.16: velocities, forces, normals) with
  `+ - += -= >>`; `Coord` (one position coordinate, unsigned 8.24 in cells, with `cell()`,
  `units()`, `Coord - Coord` = signed distance) and `Pos` (three `Coord`s, with `Pos + Vec3` and
  `Pos - Pos` = `Vec3`). Adding one position to another does not compile, which alone would
  catch the kind of int32/uint32 mix-up that used to happen. `Angle` (0x10000 = 360°, wraps
  around by itself, compares and shifts as signed like the original; `DEG45`, `DEG90`, `DEG180`)
  and `Q15` (sine/cosine and matrices; `Q15 * Q15`, `int16_t * Q15`, `neg_sat()`, `q31()`):
  `fx_sin`, `fx_cos` and `fx_atan2` use these types, as do `build_matrix`, `rotate`, the cameras
  (`Angles` with `roll`, `pitch`, `yaw`) and the steering (`Car::steer`). `.raw` gives the raw
  value where the original does arithmetic on it (shifts, 32-bit products).
- **Methods on the car.** `Car` is the `carN.dat` header with `vertices()`, `springs()` and the
  physics as methods (`car.update_springs()`, `car.jump(...)`); `CarSpring::type`/`softness()`,
  `CarVertex::is_wheel()`, `Particle::ICE_CHIP` etc. The car's model (a small bytecode program)
  is decoded at load time into a list of typed instructions, `ModelOp`, with jump and call
  targets as indices; `draw_car` runs it with a local `Program`.
- **References, `bool`, `enum`, lambdas** instead of output pointers, int flags, `#define`s and
  local macros; no `goto`.
- `#pragma once` in every header; the state structs are trivially copyable, with no
  constructors.

The structures that lived in the data segment used to be `packed`, to keep the original layout;
they are ordinary structs now (only `PcxHeader`, a file format, is still packed). Some code
still uses a copy and writes it back, or a pointer, where a reference would do now.

### Global state

The original keeps everything in one 64 KB data segment, addressed by offsets. Here the state is
a few global structures, split by subject (`terep.hpp`, each field with its original offset in a
comment): `world` (gravity, cars, players, particles), `camera`, `render` (clipping, polygons,
visible terrain, scanline tables), `map_tables` (palette, fog and translucency tables) and
`contact` (the last ground contact). `state_reset()` (`state.cpp`) gives them their initial
values. Only what really carries state from one call to the next is there: the asm's scratch
variables, and what the original passed from one function to the next through the segment (the
polygon colour, the scanline range, the terrain rows, the collision planes, the ground probe,
the camera's axes), are locals and parameters now. Some of what stayed is less obvious than it
looks: the particles of a car-vs-car push take their velocity from the last ground contact, and
the visible terrain is kept from the last frame when the view hexagon is clipped away. Besides
them: the cars, the keyboard
(`keys`), and `segments` (heightmap, colour map, textures, screen: 64 KB vectors indexed with
16-bit offsets that wrap like the original's; each car's skin is in its `Car`).

### Cars

The original copies the whole `carN.dat` into the segment and uses the file as the car structure
itself: the header holds the state (steering, throttle, wheels...), the points and springs are
read by offset and the model is a program whose counter is an offset in the segment. Here
`car_read` (`src/car_file.cpp`) parses the file into a `Car` with `std::vector`s of points and
springs and the model decoded (`model_decode`: one `ModelOp` per instruction, the program
counter becomes an index into that list). The game keeps nothing else of the file. The title bug
was fixed in `Car::jump`.

What the original read from `data.bin` is now written by code. The constants live with the code
that uses them: the texts in `game.cpp`, the file names in `terep.hpp`/`load.cpp`, the font in
`text.cpp` (read from `src/font.pbm`, embedded in the executable with `#embed`), the surface, key
and hull tables in `physics.cpp`, the sound patches in `sound.cpp`, the smoke quads in
`scene.cpp`, and the sine and atan tables computed in `math.cpp` (the atan table with a slightly
wrong π, 3.141688765, which gives exactly the original's). Until the data segment was split, it
came out byte for byte identical to the original,
which the old tests compared with the asm (see Verification).

## Verification

`make test` (`tests/run_tests.sh`) replays the recordings made with the Win16 port, one
directory per recording in `tests/` (the map is the one of its `#selected path:` line, under
`data/`), and compares the frames: every frame's hash and a few full frames.

Before that, while the data segment still had the original layout, the tests compared a CRC of
the frame buffer and of the whole data segment, per frame, with the original asm (assembled with
nasm and run in a 16-bit x86 emulator, unicorn) and with an older mechanical C++ translation:
a 600-frame scenario through every key and a dozen random scripts of 3000 frames matched,
except where the original hits the title bug, fixed here (below). That setup is in the git
history (`tools/asm_oracle`, `tests/ref`, `host_test/car_image.cpp`).

Recordings made with the Win16 port are replayed with `terep2-headless -R recdir mapdir`
(`-C` instead of `-R` only compares, writing nothing). `recdir/record.txt` has one call per line,
told apart by its first letter and made exactly as recorded at 1x: `init`, `P` (physics), `R`
(render), `K: 0xcd` (key), `frame: name.pgm` and `frame_fnv1a_64: 0x...`.

- Empty lines and lines starting with `#` are skipped. Before the first `init` nothing else is
  allowed (`... before init`, an error); after it, other lines print `unhandled line: ...`.
- `frame:` saves the frame buffer as `recdir/name_new.pgm` (P5, like the port's dumps) and
  prints how it compares with `recdir/name.pgm`: the number of differing pixels and the
  rectangle around them.
- `frame_fnv1a_64:` compares the FNV-1a hash of the frame buffer; only mismatches are printed.

The last line sums it up, and the exit code is 1 if any frame differs or has no original.

`-s N` replays at a higher scale. The recorded hashes are of 1x frames, so there they are
replaced by the port's own: `-R` writes them to `recdir/hashes_Nx.txt` (one per
`frame_fnv1a_64` line) and `-C` compares with that file, as a regression test of the higher
scales. The `frame:` images are compared by similarity instead: the average colour of each 8 x 8
block (in 1x pixels), whose mean difference must stay under 15 (the finer projection moves
edges and texels by less than a pixel; the same picture gives 1 to 10, another one over 30).
`make test` also replays every recording at each scale it has a `hashes_Nx.txt` for.

## Things found along the way

Bugs and quirks of the original that were **kept** (they are commented in the code):

- **Jump**: the search for the lowest vertex uses AX, which is the low half of the kick, so the
  low half of the kick ends up being the height of the last vertex (`physics.cpp`, `Car::jump`).
- Polygon clipping: the left/top edges skip the intersection when the previous vertex is on the
  edge; right/bottom do not. Texture interpolation in the clipper uses half the precision.
- Projection of the points cut by the near plane uses the fixed centre (160,100), even with the
  screen split.
- `find_ref_vertex` takes its iteration count from the fractional part of the first vertex's x.
- The PCX header is barely validated.

Differences that only show with unusual data: at most 5 cars are loaded (the original's name
tables hold 5, and a sixth car took its name from the bytes after them), and text characters
>= 128 use the glyph of `c & 0x7f` (the original's offsets wrapped around the data segment; only
its jump bug put such characters in the title).

Bug of the original that was **fixed**:

- **Title that gets corrupted**: holding 1/2 while switching cars (Tab/Q) kicks the
  `lowest_vertex` of a car that never jumped, which is 0 (an offset in the segment). The kick is
  added at offset 0x14 of the segment, which is the "H" of "VEHICLE" in the title, and the letter
  turns into garbage. Since letters ≥ 128 read the font table out of place, sometimes even past
  the end of `data.bin`, the corrupted title was not even the same between builds. Now such a
  car looks for its lowest point as on a fresh press, and the jump works.

Bug of the original that can be **fixed on request** (the `fix-ice-bug` option):

- **Ice pillars**: an ice chip that lands lowers the heightmap cell under it by one
  (`particles_update`). The height is a byte, so at 0 it wraps around to 255, the highest
  terrain there is (4080 units): a thin pillar appears out of the ice, keeps throwing the cars
  up, and every chip landing on it lowers it by one again. With the fix the cell stays at 0.
  The recorded tests never chip ice at height 0, so they pass with and without it.

Crash of the original that the port **does not reproduce** (left as it is):

- **Divide overflow when flying high**: projection (`project`, orig 1000:2760) divides with
  16-bit `IDIV`, so the screen coordinate has to fit in 16 bits. A point that the near-plane
  clipper puts at depth `near_clip` (30) overflows when it is more than about 3840 units
  (some 15 cells) above or below the eye. With a car kicked high up (1+2), the chase camera
  follows it and terrain triangles crossing the near plane have corners thousands of units
  below; the quotient does not fit and the CPU raises #DE, which ends the original ("divide by
  zero in 16-bit code" under Wine, with BX = 0x1e = `near_clip`). The port divides in 32 bits
  and keeps the low 16 bits, so the coordinate wraps around instead: the point lands on the
  other side of the screen and that polygon is drawn stretched across it for the frames it
  lasts. It goes back to normal once the car comes down. The same happens at any scale, since
  `near_point` projects before scaling. The tests never get there.

Difference between the Win16 port and `previous_effort`: the spring length (`sqrt`) is rounded
(CVTSS2SI) in the binary, while previous_effort truncated it. That is why it drifted from the
original after a few hundred frames.

## Not done

- There is no Win16/DOS build; the target is portable C++.

# SkyNET SDL

An unofficial, open-source C# + SDL3 port of *The Terminator: SkyNET* (Bethesda Softworks, 1996)
that also plays *The Terminator: Future Shock*, with a mission editor (`SkyNetEdit`).

Unofficial fan port. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Bethesda Softworks, ZeniMax or the owners
of The Terminator. **No game data is included.**

## Download

[Releases](https://github.com/nautilusbits/skynet-sdl/releases): Windows, Linux and macOS
builds (the game `skynet-sdl` and the editor `SkyNetEdit`), the Android APK and the optional HD mod
`skynet-hd.zip`. The Linux and macOS builds come from GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/release.yml`);
macOS builds are unsigned (`xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <folder>` once). The game's data is not included: you need your own copy (below).

## Screenshots

### The original DOS look, and ENHANCED

### SkyNetEdit

### Future Shock

## You need

A legal copy of SkyNET v1.01 and/or Future Shock: the folder holding `MDMDMAP2.BSA` (SkyNET) or
`MDMDMAPS.BSA` (Future Shock). Future Shock's data is found beside SkyNET's where the installer puts
it (`shock/GAMEDATA`).

## Installing

The port replaces the DOS executable only: it reads the game's own data files and never changes them.

**Windows**

1. Install SkyNET (from its CD, or copy an existing install). You need the folder with the game's
   data, usually `GAMEDATA`, holding `MDMDMAP2.BSA`.
2. Unzip `skynet-sdl-<version>-win-x64.zip` into the game's folder, beside `GAMEDATA`:
   ```
   SKYNET\
     GAMEDATA\          SkyNET's data (MDMDMAP2.BSA, ...)
     shock\
       GAMEDATA\        Future Shock's data (MDMDMAPS.BSA, ...), optional
     mods\              mods (skynet-hd.zip, ...); the port creates it
     saves\             saved games; settings sit beside the exe
     skynet-sdl.exe     the port
     SkyNetEdit.exe     the editor
   ```
3. Run `skynet-sdl.exe`. The first start prepares the maps once ("PREPARING GAME DATA").

Future Shock is found in `shock\GAMEDATA` beside SkyNET's data folder (the original installer's
layout) and then shows up under NEW GAME. `mods\` is always beside the exe (`--mods-dir <folder>`
to move it). The data can live anywhere else: start with `skynet-sdl.exe --data <folder>` or set
`SKYNET_DATA`.

**Linux / macOS**

Unpack the `.tar.gz` the same way, beside the data folder, and run `./skynet-sdl`.
Linux needs glibc 2.35+ and a Vulkan driver. macOS builds are unsigned: run
`xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <folder>` once.

**Android**

1. Copy the game's data folder (the one holding `MDMDMAP2.BSA`) to the phone.
2. Install `SkyNET-<version>.apk` (allow installing from this source when asked).
3. On the first start, pick that folder: the app copies it into its own storage.
   Long-press the app icon → Setup to change it later or to pick a mods folder.

**HD mod (optional)**

Copy `skynet-hd.zip` (unzipped or not) into `mods\` beside the exe and turn it on under
OPTIONS → MODS.

## Running

```
skynet-sdl.exe --data <the game's data folder>
```

Without `--data` the game tries `SKYNET_DATA`, then `gamedata` beside the exe or
its parent. The first start bakes the maps ("PREPARING GAME DATA").

Android: on the first start the app asks for the game's folder and copies it into its own storage.

Main options (`skynet-sdl.exe --help` lists all):

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--data <dir>` | the game's data folder |
| `--mission N` / `--map N` | start mission N / on MAP.NNN |
| `--mod <name>[,name]` / `--no-mods` | mods for this run / none |
| `--look original\|enhanced` | DOS look or the enhanced renderer |
| `--gpu d3d12\|vulkan` | the graphics backend |
| `--width N --height N`, `--fullscreen` | the window |
| `--difficulty low\|med\|high` | robots' fire rate and damage |
| `--host=MAP.NNN` / `--join=HOST[:PORT]` | network deathmatch ([docs/multiplayer.md](docs/multiplayer.md)) |
| `--dedicated --config server.json` | dedicated server (`config/server.sample.json`) |
| `--record NAME` / `--playdemo NAME` | demos ([docs/demos.md](docs/demos.md)) |

## Building

.NET 10 SDK. Packages come from nuget.org; the engine (`RetroEng.*`) from its public feed
(`nuget.config`: https://nautilusbits.github.io/retroeng-packages/index.json).

```
dotnet build SkyNet.slnx
```

| Target | Command | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Release (Native AOT) | `build-release.bat` → `release\skynet-sdl.exe` (`-r linux-x64` for Linux) | VS C++ tools; Vulkan SDK optional (Vulkan/Metal shaders) |
| Editor | `build-editor.bat` | |
| Android | `build-android.bat` → `release-android\SkyNET-<version>.apk` | android workload, Android SDK, JDK 21, Vulkan SDK |

The release publish by hand: `dotnet publish src\SkyNet.App\SkyNet.App.csproj -c Release -r win-x64 -o release`.

Engine work: with a RetroEng checkout at `..\..\retroeng` (or `RetroEngRoot`), build with
`-p:UseLocalRetroEng=true` to use project references instead of the `RetroEng.*` packages.

| Project | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `SkyNet.App` / `SkyNet.Android` / `SkyNet.Edit` | Game executable (desktop, Android) and mission editor. |
| `SkyNet.Game`, `SkyNet.Data`, `SkyNet.Formats` | Game logic, extracted tables, DOS file formats. |
| `SkyNet.Upscale` | Optional texture upscaling through an external Real-ESRGAN (ncnn/Vulkan) tool. |

## Tests

```
dotnet test -c Release
```

Set `SKYNET_DATA=<the SkyNET data folder>` for the tests that need the game's data; without it they
are skipped. Future Shock tests also need its data beside SkyNET's.

## Mods

Mods live in `mods/` beside the exe and are turned on under OPTIONS - MODS or with `--mod`.
[docs/modding.md](docs/modding.md) is the reference; `mods-samples/` holds small examples.
The HD pack **skynet-hd** (`skynet-hd.zip` on the Releases page; unzip into `mods/` or copy the zip there)
is released separately under **CC BY-NC 4.0** (non-commercial, own credits).

## Licence

MIT (see `LICENSE`) for the port's code, docs and sample mods. Third-party components:
`THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`. `data/tables` holds values read from the original SKYNET.EXE v1.01,
included for interoperability; `tools/SkyNet.Tables` rebuilds them from your own copy. The licence
grants no rights to the original games or their data.

The engine, RetroEng, is not part of this repository: its `RetroEng.*` packages are binary-only
under the RetroEng Non-Commercial Binary Licence (`LICENSE-RetroEng.txt` in each package). Builds
that ship the engine may be shared free of charge but not used commercially (no sales, paid access
or advertising) without the engine's copyright holder's written permission. SkyNET, Future Shock, Bethesda and The
Terminator are trademarks of their owners.

# wc-decomp

Decompiles Wing Commander's `WC.EXE` (and the Secret Missions 2's `SM2.EXE`) to C with Ghidra,
driven from TypeScript, and recompiles it into a native or WebAssembly program.

## Building it yourself

This repository contains no game files and nothing derived from them: you need your own copy of
Wing Commander, the GOG release (with the Secret Missions). Everything is worked out on its
`WC.EXE`, SHA-256 `c37d085909175abc95b4a51ffc884913c7d4ea52ba66ca932619ce1f67fa91ca`, and `SM2.EXE`,
`900f379b04c7b6f11ae08cf84ca278b9260df8ed81d038cdb3907bbf136cd84d`; other releases are refused. The
native build runs on macOS.

Prerequisites (Homebrew):

```bash
brew install node ghidra cmake ninja sdl3   # Node 23.6 or later; Ghidra 12.2 brings its JDK
brew install emscripten                     # only for the web page (npm run web)
git submodule update --init                 # Nuked-OPL3, for AdLib sound
npm ci
```

Then, with the game folder (the one with `WC.EXE` and `GAMEDAT/`) at `../game`, or passing
`-- --exe path/to/WC.EXE` to every step:

```bash
npm run decompile    # flatten the overlays, analyze with Ghidra (a few minutes)
npm run recomp       # generate C from it and build out/bin/wc
npm run discover     # run it: captures and recompiles the drivers the game loads (a few minutes)
out/bin/wc ../game   # play (arguments after the folder go to the game: Origin -k, the developers'
                     # mode, makes your ship take no damage; "Origin" spelled exactly so)
```

The Secret Missions 2 are a program of their own, `SM2.EXE`: the same steps with `-- --game sm2`
build `out/sm2/bin/sm2` (everything generated for it goes to `out/sm2/`; its entry points are in
`entries-sm2.txt`):

```bash
npm run decompile -- --game sm2 && npm run recomp -- --game sm2 && npm run discover -- --game sm2
out/sm2/bin/sm2 ../game
```

After its intro, `SM2.EXE` asks a copy-protection question on a black screen ("Enter 5:"): in GOG's
release the question isn't shown and any answer is accepted, so type anything and press Enter.

Everything generated goes to `out/` (ignored by git). `discover` runs the game headless several
times; the drivers it captures depend on the game's sound setting (`WINGCMDR.CFG`, written by the
game's installer; AdLib music is what's tested). The Borland runtime libraries are optional (see
"Naming the Borland runtime" below); they only give the decompiled C nicer names.

`WC.EXE` is a 16-bit DOS program built with Borland Turbo C++ (1990) that keeps more than half
its code in Borland VROOM overlays (an `FBOV` block after the MZ image). Ghidra's MZ loader
ignores those overlays, so the pipeline first **flattens** the EXE:

1. `src/vroom.ts` parses the FBOV header, Borland's segment table and the 40 overlay stubs.
2. `src/flatten.ts` appends each overlay's code to the image as a new segment, adds its
   relocations to the MZ table and rewrites every `int 3Fh` stub entry into a `jmp far` to the
   real function. The result, `out/WC_FLAT.EXE`, is for analysis only and won't run under DOS.
3. `ghidra_scripts/WcSetup.java` (pre-analysis) sets `DS` to DGROUP in all code and names the
   overlay entry points `ovlNN_xxxx`, with a comment giving the original stub address. It also
   turns off Ghidra's "Decompiler Switch Analysis" (see step 5).
4. Ghidra auto-analysis runs.
5. `ghidra_scripts/WcSwitches.java` recovers `switch` jump tables (`jmp cs:[bx+table]`).
   Ghidra's 16-bit x86 model takes CS to be the instruction address rounded down to 64 KB, so
   its own switch analysis reads these tables from the wrong place and creates bogus code and
   functions. The script reads each table from the real segment, disassembles the cases, merges
   back function fragments that analysis split off (loop and case bodies reached by `JMP`s that
   Ghidra turned into fake tail calls), and stores a jump-table override for the decompiler.
   It also turns off Ghidra's "Shared Return Calls" analyzer, which would otherwise split those
   functions again during headless post-analysis. The tables are saved to `out/switches.json`.
6. `ghidra_scripts/WcFid.java` applies the Borland Function ID database (see below), if it
   exists, and turns link names into C names (`_printf` → `printf`).
7. `ghidra_scripts/WcRuntime.java` names the Borland runtime functions that Function ID didn't
   match (or all of them, without the database) by rules:
   `main`/`exit` and `_argc`/`_argv`/`_environ` from the startup code, `atexit`, `abort`,
   `__IOerror`/`errno`, thin DOS wrappers by their `INT 21h` function (`_open`, `_read`, `lseek`, …),
   and compiler helpers (`SCOPY@`, `LXMUL@`, `LDIV@`, …) by a hash of their code bytes. It also marks
   `exit`, `_exit` and `abort` as non-returning and removes the bogus code Ghidra decoded after
   calls to them. Each name gets a plate comment saying which rule produced it; functions you
   have already renamed are left alone.
8. `ghidra_scripts/WcDecompile.java` decompiles every function into `out/c/`, one file per
   original segment (`code_XXXX.c`, `ovlNN.c`), plus `functions.tsv` and `ghidra_types.h`.
   For the recovered switches, the decompiler only knows the case targets, so it prints
   `switch(*(table + i*2)) { case 0x3505b: …`. Using `switches.json`, the script prints them as
   `switch(i) { case 0: case 1: …` instead, folding Borland's `i - N` bias into the case values.

## Usage

Ghidra is found via `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR` or `ghidraRun` on `PATH`.

```bash
npm run decompile            # flatten + import + analyze + export C (takes a few minutes)
npm run flatten              # only build out/WC_FLAT.EXE and out/manifest.json
npm run redecompile          # re-export C from the existing project
```

Pass `-- --exe path/to/WC.EXE --out dir` to change the input or output location.

### Naming the Borland runtime with Function ID

`WC.EXE` was built with Turbo C++ 1.0 in the medium memory model. To have Ghidra recognise its
runtime library by code, put these files from a Turbo C++ 1.0 install in one folder (by default
`../tc/extracted`; they're in `MLIB.ZIP` and `XLIB.ZIP` on the install disks) and run, once:

```bash
npm run fid -- --borland path/to/folder
```

| File | Contains |
|---|---|
| `CM.LIB` (required) | the medium-model C runtime |
| `C0M.OBJ` | the medium-model startup code |
| `OVERLAY.LIB` | the VROOM overlay manager |

This imports the libraries into `out/borland` and builds `out/borland-tc10.fidb`; later
`npm run decompile` runs apply it. The database is only registered with Ghidra while a script uses it.

The Ghidra project is saved in `out/ghidra/WC.gpr`. Open it in the Ghidra GUI to rename
functions, define structs and fix types, then run `npm run redecompile` to regenerate the C
with your names.

## A native macOS executable (static recompilation)

`npm run recomp` translates the analyzed program into C that compiles: `ghidra_scripts/WcRecomp.java`
turns every instruction's p-code into C working on an emulated 8086 state (`runtime/wc_rt.h`), one
C function per Ghidra function, and CMake (`CMakeLists.txt`, build tree in `out/build/`) compiles it,
together with the runtime in `runtime/`, into `out/bin/wc` (`brew install cmake ninja sdl3`).

```bash
npm run recomp               # generate out/recomp/*.c and build out/bin/wc
npm run build                # only rebuild (cmake --build out/build)
npm run discover             # run it; add code reached only through pointers in data, rebuild, repeat
out/bin/wc ../game           # run (WC_TRACE=1 traces DOS calls, WC_TRACE=2 every instruction)
```

The runtime (`runtime/`) loads and relocates the program image like DOS would (`WC_LOAD_SEG`,
default `0200`) and provides a small DOS on top of the game folder: files, current directory,
memory, vectors, date and time, and expanded memory (EMS, 8 MB, as in GOG's DOSBox; `WC_EMS=0`
turns it off: the game then keeps everything in conventional memory, and its music could stall). Hardware interrupts are emulated (8259 PIC,
8253 timer at the rate the game programs, keyboard from the terminal or `WC_KEYS`), every vector
starts at a native BIOS entry (F000:nn), and `INT n` goes through the vector table, so the game's
own handlers run. BIOS video, keyboard and mouse services are stubs. Generator
details that matter:

- Ghidra's 16-bit model computes CS as the address rounded down to 64 KB and drops some segment
  override prefixes; the generator substitutes the real segment and the prefix's register.
- Values from MZ relocations become `value + wc_reloc`, so the image can load at any segment.
- Calls keep a shadow return stack, so a jump to the expected return address (Borland's
  `_setargv` returns that way) is a return.
- Every overlay stub entry, plus the addresses in `entries.txt`, is decoded with Ghidra's
  pseudo-disassembler, since such code is often missing or misaligned in the listing.
- The VROOM overlay manager still initialises as on DOS (it opens WC.EXE and reserves its
  buffer, though the overlays are resident); the game's INT 21h hook depends on its state.

### Code loaded at runtime (drivers)

The game unpacks its Origin FX drivers (`TM.DRV`, `SUPERTM.DRV`, ... are compressed containers) into
the heap and calls them through far pointers. `npm run discover` handles that too: when the
program calls into memory that isn't program code, the runtime saves the 64 KB segment
(`out/loaded/`), discover imports it into the Ghidra project at its own 64 KB-aligned virtual
segment (6000, 7000, ..., by a hash of the driver in `drivers.txt`, since the game loads them in no
fixed order; `WcDriverEntries.java` seeds the entry points and only reachable code is
decoded), and `WcRecomp.java driver` recompiles it as position-independent code. At runtime a
driver is recognised by its instruction bytes wherever it is loaded, and writes into those bytes
(self-modifying code) are reported; none have been seen.

Overlay code reads its own constants (switch tables) through CS from a pristine copy of the
image, since the heap overlaps the flattened overlays' addresses at runtime.

### The window

`out/bin/wc` opens a window (SDL3) showing the mode 13h picture at
4:3, and passes the keyboard to the game as PC scancodes (the arrow and other grey keys as their
keypad twins) and the mouse to a mouse driver (INT 33h, `runtime/mouse.c`; the game draws its own
pointer, so the Mac's is hidden over the window). In full screen the pointer is captured, so the
menu bar and the Dock don't pop up at the screen edges; the game gets the mouse's movement, twice
as fast as the picture is wide; Cmd+Left/Right change that by 25% (`WC_MOUSE_SPEED` sets it; the title
shows it, and in full screen the terminal). Cmd+F toggles full screen, Cmd+Q quits. The recompiled program runs on a thread of
its own; the window shows the frame buffer and palette as they were at the last vertical retrace,
which runs at the VGA's 70 Hz in real time (port 3DAh). `runtime/host.h` is the whole interface
between the two, so the emulation itself never includes SDL.

Wing Commander paces its animation and space flight by CPU speed, so the runtime limits it to
8334 instructions per millisecond. Cmd+Up/Down in the window change that by 20% (the title shows
the value); `WC_CYCLES=n` sets it at start (instructions per ms, like DOSBox's `cycles`), and
`WC_CYCLES=max` runs as fast as possible. In space flight the game draws more per frame when
enemies are close, so there the runtime paces frames instead: 15 per second (`WC_FPS`), running
at full speed in between; in flight Cmd+Up/Down change the frame rate instead, by 20% too, and
leave the instruction rate alone. `WC_STATS=1` prints the frame rate.

`WC_HEADLESS=1` runs without a window (`npm run discover` does), taking keys from the terminal or
`WC_KEYS`. `WC_SCREENSHOT=file` saves the VGA palette and frame buffer when the program stops (also
on Ctrl-C or a timeout); `tools/screenshot.py file out.png` makes a PNG.

Sound: AdLib music. The OPL2 at ports 388h/389h is emulated by
[Nuked-OPL3](https://github.com/nukeykt/Nuked-OPL3) (LGPL 2.1, a git submodule in
`third_party/`: after cloning, `git submodule update --init`); `runtime/opl.c` makes the samples in
real time and the window plays them through SDL3. `WC_WAV=file.wav` also records them (works
headless too).

Not supported yet: text-mode output, Roland MT-32 and Sound Blaster digital sound, joystick.

### Starting at any mission

`npm run mission` writes a save game that starts at a chosen mission into a free slot of the
game's `GAMEDAT/SAVEGAME.WLD` (copying the file to `SAVEGAME.BAK` first), or, for the Secret
Missions 2, `CRUSADE.WLD` (`CRUSADE.BAK`). In the game, choose
"Continue Campaign", click the sleeping pilot of that slot in the barracks, then leave through the
right-hand door for the briefing.

```bash
npm run mission -- --list                 # the mission trees of the Vega campaign and Secret Missions 1 and 2
npm run mission -- gimle.2                # series by its system's name (or number), mission from 1
npm run mission -- sm1:midgard.1 --name Blair --callsign Maverick
npm run mission -- sm2:4.1                # Secret Missions 2 (series by number: their names repeat)
npm run mission -- --transfer 7 sm2:1.1   # the pilot of SAVEGAME.WLD's slot 7 into the Secret Missions 2
npm run mission -- --slot 3 venice.4      # needed when no slot is free: overwrites slot 3
npm run mission -- --slot 6 --move gateway.1  # move that save game there, keeping its pilot
```

The save holds a new pilot's state (taken from `WC.EXE` or `SM2.EXE`, as the game copies it when a campaign
starts) with a series history along a path through the tree, preferring won series; scores, kills,
medals and rank are those of a new pilot. `--game dir` picks another game folder, `--title` the
name shown in the barracks. `--transfer n` takes the pilot (kills, rank, medals, and the wingmen)
from slot `n` of `SAVEGAME.WLD` instead, like the game's own converters `TRANSFER.EXE` and
`TRANS2.EXE` (which aren't recompiled, and accept only pilots from Venice or the Secret Missions);
the save is named after that slot's.

## In the browser (WebAssembly)

The same runtime builds with [Emscripten](https://emscripten.org) (`brew install emscripten`) into a
web page: `runtime/host_web.c` takes the place of the SDL window, and `web/index.html` shows the
picture on a canvas (full screen with ⌘/Ctrl+F or the button; the pointer is captured there), passes
the keyboard and mouse to the game and plays the AdLib music with an AudioWorklet.

```bash
npm run recomp && npm run discover   # as for the native build, if not done yet
npm run web                          # out/web: index.html, wc.js, wc.wasm, sw.js
npm run web -- --game sm2            # adds sm2.js, sm2.wasm: the page offers the Secret Missions 2 too
npm run serve                        # http://localhost:8080
```

On the page, drop your game folder (or choose it, or its files): the files are kept in the browser's
IndexedDB, so this is needed once. Whatever the game writes (save games, high scores, in
`SAVEGAME.WLD`) goes to IndexedDB as well and is there again after a reload, also when you give the
page the game files anew; "Download save games" makes a copy. The page asks the browser to keep its
storage persistent, but a browser may still clear it, so keep copies of save games you care about.
Logs go to the browser console; URL parameters set the `WC_*` variables (`?WC_STATS=1`), and
`?args=` the game's command line (`?args=Origin%20-k`).

The emulation runs on a thread of its own, which needs `SharedArrayBuffer`, so the page has to be
cross-origin isolated: `npm run serve` sends the headers for that, and on a static host that can't,
`sw.js` adds them (the page reloads once). The built page contains the recompiled game, so like
`out/bin/wc` it's for your own use, not for publishing.

## Expect pseudocode, not compilable C

The output reads like C but won't compile: it has no original names or types, it uses
segment arithmetic and Ghidra helpers such as `CONCAT22`, and it touches DOS and hardware
directly (`int 21h`, VGA memory, ports). Treat it as the starting point for a rewrite.

## License

BSD 2-Clause (`LICENSE`), for this repository's code. Nuked-OPL3 (`third_party/`, linked into
`out/bin/wc`) is LGPL 2.1. Wing Commander itself is not included and remains its owners' property.

﻿# F-117A Nighthawk Stealth Fighter 2.0 — SDL3 port

A faithful native port of MicroProse's *F-117A Nighthawk Stealth Fighter 2.0* (1991) in C with SDL3. It is not an
emulator: the game's logic is re-implemented function by function, and the port reads the original game files at
run time. The release does not contain the game. You need your own copy.

An enhanced version (higher resolution, a wider view, later a higher frame rate; the original art unchanged):
[F117-2Enhanced](https://github.com/kylofon/F117-2Enhanced) (v0.1.0 released).

Version 0.1.0 (first release, Windows x64). What changed and what is still open: [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

## How to play

1. **You need the original game.** Its files, copied from your own installation: `F117.COM`, `SETUP.EXE`,
   `MPS_LOGO.EXE`, `PLAYER.EXE`, `START.EXE`, `VGAME.EXE`, `END.EXE`, `DSWAP.EXE`, `MGRAPHIC.EXE`, `MISC.EXE`, and
   the data files that come with them. The launcher checks the list above and tells you which one is missing.
2. **Unzip** `F117-SDL3-v0.1.0-win64.zip` into a folder of your choice.
3. **Copy the game files into `Game`**, the folder beside `F-117A Nighthawk.exe` (it is in the zip, with a
   `PUT_GAME_FILES_HERE.txt` note in it). The folder must be writable: the game saves your pilot roster there.
4. **Run `F-117A Nighthawk.exe`** and press **Play**. The launcher stays open; the game starts in its own window.
5. **SETUP** (the first program): answer **N** for the joystick and **2** for AdLib (the sound card the port
   plays). Then the intro, the title, START: create a pilot, pick a mission and launch.

The keyboard is the main input. A joystick is supported; the mouse and the joystick in the shell and the debrief
are not yet tested (see the CHANGELOG).

### The launcher

`F-117A Nighthawk.exe` sets the options and starts `f117.exe`. Everything is remembered in
`%APPDATA%\F-117A Nighthawk\settings.ini`; delete the file to go back to the defaults.

* **Game files**: **Folder** (default `Game` beside the launcher) and **Program** (`f117.exe` beside it). The line
  under them names what is missing. **Play** stays greyed out until both are there. The (i) icon next to the
  folder's Browse button is a reminder that the folder must be writable.
* **Aspect**: 4:3, as on a VGA monitor (the default), or 1:1 square pixels.
* **Window size** and **Start in full screen**. Alt+Enter switches full screen in the game.
* **Sound**: off starts the game without sound.
* **Game speed** (default **7**): the original paces itself to about 17 frames a second on any fast PC, which makes
  radar dishes spin far too fast. The value is the number of timer ticks (70 a second) that each frame takes at
  least: 7 gives about 10 frames a second. The flight model is scaled to the measured rate, so the aircraft still
  flies at the same speed. **0** is the original pacing, the fast spin of the original on today's PCs.
* **Key Bindings...**: every action of the game with its key, on four tabs (Flying, Weapons and countermeasures,
  Views, Displays and game). Click a key's button, press the new key (Shift, Ctrl and Alt can be held with it).
  **Reset to defaults**, **OK**, **Cancel**. Changed keys are shown in bold and saved in `settings.ini`. The keys that cannot be changed are listed under
  **Static keys**.
* Hover over an option for a short explanation.
* **About**: version, author and links.

### Main keys (defaults)

| Action | Key |
|---|---|
| Stick (pitch and roll) | keypad arrows (the grey cursor keys) |
| Throttle up / down; full / idle | `=` / `-`; Shift+`=` / Shift+`-` |
| Gear / flaps / bay doors / autopilot | `6` / `9` / `8` / `7` |
| Wheel brakes / eject | `0` / Shift+F10 |
| Select weapon / gun / release | Space / Backspace / Enter |
| Flare / chaff / IR jammer / ECM jammer / decoy | `1` / `2` / `3` / `4` / `5` |
| Drop targets / master mode | `B` / F2 |
| Views: front / chase / zoom in and out | F1 / Shift+F1 / `Z` / `X` |
| Look left / right / rear / ahead | `M` / `,` / `.` / `/` |
| MFDs: left / weapons / FLIR / nav / page | F3 / F5 / F6 / F7 / F10 |
| HUD mode / HUD style | `V` / `C` |
| Pause / sound on and off | Alt+`P` / Alt+`V` |

Alt+Q, Alt+B, Alt+S and Alt+Enter keep their jobs in the game. The launcher's Key Bindings dialog lists the rest
(56 actions in all) and is the place to change them.

### Saves, logs and errors

* **Pilot roster**: `Game\ROSTER.FIL`, written by the game like the original.
* **Errors**: `f117.log` beside `f117.exe` gets one dated line for each error the game reports. Attach it to a bug
  report.

### Command line

The launcher runs `f117.exe`; you can also run it directly. The usual options:

```text
f117 [--game-dir DIR] [--scale N] [--aspect 4:3|1:1] [--fullscreen] [--headless]
     [--trace] [--check] [--chain-test] [--tick-test [MS]] [--keys NAME=CODE,...]
     [--frame-ticks N] [--keymap-test] [--version]
```

* `--game-dir DIR`: the folder with the original files (default `Game`).
* `--scale N`: the window is 320x240 times N (default 3). `--aspect 4:3|1:1` and `--fullscreen` as in the launcher.
* `--frame-ticks N`: the game speed (default 7; 0 = the original pacing).
* `--keys NAME=CODE,...`: key bindings for the actions not on their defaults (the launcher passes its changes this way).
* `--check`: checks that the game folder holds the files the game needs and exits.
* `--trace`: prints the program switches and their exit codes (also `F117_TRACE=1`).
* `--headless`: no window and no sound, for tests. `--version` prints the version and exits.

The remaining test options are listed at the top of `f117port/src/main.c`.

## Building

MSYS2 `mingw64` (gcc, ninja, cmake, and the packages `mingw-w64-x86_64-sdl3`,
`mingw-w64-x86_64-wxwidgets3.2-msw` for the launcher). The release is made by one script:

```bash
python tools/make_release.py     # clean Release build with the launcher, ctest, the zip in release/
```

or by hand:

```bash
cmake -S f117port -B f117port/build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++ -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DF117_LAUNCHER=ON
cmake --build f117port/build && ctest --test-dir f117port/build
f117port/build/f117 --game-dir Game
```

`-DF117_LAUNCHER=OFF` (the default) skips the launcher. The tests that need the game files skip themselves when
`Game` is not there. Details: [f117port/PORTING.md](f117port/PORTING.md) and [f117port/launcher/README.md](f117port/launcher/README.md).

## For developers: how the port was made

The port is a reverse-engineering project, not a translation of source code (MicroProse never published any).
The original DOS programs are disassembled and traced; their behaviour is written down as specifications, and the
C code is checked against the original under emulation, function by function.

```text
Game\        junction to the installed DOS game (not in git)
_tools\      junction to Ghidra + JDK (shared with the other ports, not in git)
tools\       reverse-engineering scripts (Python, Ghidra) and tools\make_release.py
port\        RE guide, function indexes, symbols, specs (port\spec), formats (port\formats)
f117port\    the port: src\ (C, SDL3), launcher\ (wxWidgets), tests (ctest), PORTING.md
licenses\    third-party licence texts for the DLLs in the zip
docs\        manual PDFs/text (not in git)
work\        generated output and DOSBox reference captures (not in git)
release\     the zip and its staged folder (not in git)
```

* `PLAN.md`: the state of the port, the subtasks and the open checks by the user. The rules for the agents that
  worked on it are in `CLAUDE.md`; `FORMATS.md` describes the file formats.
* `port/spec/`: the specifications the port follows.
* Game data is never committed or zipped: `Game\` is ignored by git, and `make_release.py` refuses to stage any
  original game file.

## Licence

The code in this repository is MIT (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). The third-party libraries in the zip (SDL3, Nuked-OPL3,
wxWidgets and the DLLs they need) have their own licences; the texts are in `licenses\`, and the list is in
[licenses/THIRD-PARTY.md](licenses/THIRD-PARTY.md). F-117A Nighthawk Stealth Fighter 2.0 is © MicroProse; this
project is not affiliated with it and contains none of its files.

# ROLLER

[![CI][ci-shd]][ci-url] [![LC][lc-shd]][lc-url] [![Download][dl-shd]][dl-url]
[![Play in your browser][web-shd]][web-url]

https://fatal.racing/

![Roller logo](./images/whiplash.gif)

This project aims to implement all the functionality of the 1995 game
Whiplash/Fatal Racing in a way that builds and runs on modern PCs. Where
necessary, DOS-specific functions are substituted with SDL and Windows/Unix
equivalents. For instruction-matching decomp, see
https://github.com/FatalDecomp/ROLLER-matching

[![On track!](https://img.youtube.com/vi/JvoiQTRjt88/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JvoiQTRjt88)

## Play

**[Play ROLLER in your browser][web-url]** with the bundled freeware demo, or
import an image of a legally owned retail disc for the full game. No install is
required.

Native installations require assets from a retail copy of the game. Download the
latest native version from the
[releases](https://github.com/FatalDecomp/ROLLER/releases) page and extract it
wherever you want. On initial launch, select a CD image (CUE/BIN or ISO) to
extract the assets. Press the \` key to access additional settings.

## About

Debug symbol dump generated with wdump, part of:
https://github.com/open-watcom/open-watcom-v2

Useful tool in generating nice asm output with symbols from wdump applied:
https://github.com/fonic/wcdatool

Directions on how to use wcdatool and get remote debugging working with open
watcom: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bG9tEZOSrQg

Note: wdump symbol offsets do not account for DOS4GW.EXE. Load
FATAL.EXE_split_dos4g_payload.exe (FATAL.EXE with DOS4GW.EXE split off,
generated by wcdatool) into Ida/Ghidra to have matching symbol offsets.

Hashes of executables used for decomp:

FATAL.EXE

- `md5: 812EEE1404ECDFD87FF765281DF89720`
- `SHA256: 7789768C0A6CDC213EAF7B1AD8CC125531EB3FE7C213ECCAC6188E58F428687E`

FATAL.EXE_split_dos4g_payload.exe

- `md5: 05C2B0730641663133D76DD2CA552B4C`
- `SHA256: A4AD4131DBBFF9884DA4687D8B579B81117E6D23525950D942DF2DF585E2A11E`

## External Dependencies Used:

- SDL3.2.22: https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL
- SDL_Image3.2.4: https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL_image
- WildMIDI 0.4.6: https://github.com/Mindwerks/wildmidi
- libcdio-2.3.0: https://github.com/libcdio/libcdio
- Nuklear 4.13.2: https://github.com/Immediate-Mode-UI/Nuklear

## Build

Video instructions: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QEDGhvvZ9XU

### Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zizin13/roller.git
cd roller
```

### Install prerequisites

- [Zig 0.15.2](https://ziglang.org/download/)

The easiest way to install is to use [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/):

```bash
mise install
```

### Build and run the project

Using default settings

```bash
zig build run
```

A custom data folder

```bash
zig build -Dassets-path=/path/to/fatdata run
```

### Prepare the playable demo assets

The browser build uses the hash-pinned Whiplash demo selected by ADR 0002.
`zig build web` automatically downloads, verifies, and extracts only its
`FATDATA` tree before packaging it at `/demo/fatdata`:

```bash
zig build web
```

For an offline build, prepare the tree from a previously downloaded copy, then
point the web build at it. The explicit tree is verified against the same E3.S2
file count, size, and tree SHA-256 before `emcc` runs:

```bash
python scripts/fetch_demo_assets.py --source /path/to/whipdemo.zip
zig build web -Ddemo-assets-path=zig-out/fatdata-demo
```

The bundle contains `roller-<sha256>.data` plus a deterministic
`bundle-manifest.json` with raw byte sizes and SHA-256 hashes.

## Testing

### Rendering snapshot tests

```bash
git lfs install        # one-time, the baselines are LFS-tracked
zig build test-snapshots
```

Captures the indexed framebuffer of every intro replay at hand-picked ticks and
runs `git diff` against the checked-in baselines. Any pixel change shows up as a
tracked-file diff that GitHub renders as a side-by-side image diff in PRs.

On a non-canonical host (anything other than the pinned reference machine) use
`-Dscratch` to capture into `zig-out/snapshot-scratch/` without touching the
LFS-tracked baselines.

See [`tests/snapshots/README.md`](tests/snapshots/README.md) for the full
developer workflow (blessing intentional pixel changes, troubleshooting, etc.)
and
[`docs/adr/0001-rendering-snapshot-tests.md`](docs/adr/0001-rendering-snapshot-tests.md)
for the policy decisions.
