# Goldbox Engine (working title)

An open-source, GPL-3.0-or-later-licensed, OpenXcom-inspired framework for playing and enhancing classic SSI Gold Box RPGs **using original resources supplied by the player**.

**Status: bounded exploration pilot.** M1 journal mods, installation scanning,
DAX/GEO/ECL decoding, selector routing, a minimal ECL VM, and terminal exploration
with state persistence are implemented. A standalone Pool of Radiance map/event
has been exercised against user-owned Steam resources. Full campaign startup,
combat, complete original-asset rendering, and embedded JS remain unimplemented; game compatibility is
still unverified. See the [local validation scope](docs/research/local-validation-2026-10-15.md).

## What actually works today

- Buildable, testable C++20 engine and console demonstration.
- JSON importer for **independently authored synthetic sample content only**.
- Load real `mod.json` files from disk, validate schemas and field types, and patch journal titles or text.
- Apply mod dependencies deterministically, with explicit conflict warnings and cycle/missing-dependency detection.
- Select **Classic Mode** (original unpatched content) or **Enhanced Mode** (overlay mods).
- Output session metadata with game identifier, mode, and applied mod IDs/versions; **not a full savegame**.
- TypeScript types for mod authoring; **compiled JS execution is not implemented**.
- Reject symlinked mod directories/manifests, invalid IDs, oversized JSON files, and unknown manifest fields.
- Read-only installation inventory with filenames, sizes, SHA-256, resource families and decoder diagnostics.
- Shared DAX index/RLE and GEO16 decoders exercised against one local Pool of Radiance installation; public tests remain synthetic.
- ECL typed operands, five lifecycle entries and bounded selector-table routing; unsupported/state-dependent static routes remain unresolved.
- Minimal deterministic ECL VM with typed memory, conditional branches, subroutines, text, menus, indexed memory reads and combat host callbacks.
- Terminal map movement and local save/restore, including original-event output and persisted menu state in one standalone map/ECL pair.
- Profile-selected dungeon map loading through an explicit resource resolver, with map-aware save/restore; original map-18 initialization now completes in a read-only map/wall resource probe. Campaign/program switching and graphical parity remain unfinished.
- Optional SDL3 window with original/enhanced presentation modes over shared game state. Pool defaults to a native-sized scene, imported frame symbols and separate text/party regions; enhanced retains the map overview. Exact screen parity remains unfinished; see [renderer controls and limits](runtime/README.md).
- SSI EGA tile and wall-definition decoding with explicit wall-bank rendering; original archive checks pass for one Pool installation, while automatic visual bindings and scene parity remain unverified.
- Monochrome tile strips and independent/XOR-first picture/sprite decoding, with explicit palette policies; checked against local Pool picture, sprite and combat-image archives. An opt-in ECL host displays profile-timed pictures and non-replacement sprites from explicitly selected archives; original timing and scene parity remain unverified.
- Startup party creation with data-selected races/classes/alignments, bounded ability rolling, roster review/removal and engine-save persistence; see [supported creation rules and limits](docs/character-creation.md).
- Profile-selected read-only ECL party access: loaded-character selection, names, ability scores and party count; unsupported fields/writes fail explicitly. Original character-access parity remains unverified.
- WHO party-selection prompts use existing window/terminal/automation menus and update the profile-configured selected-PC byte as well as the loaded character. Original interaction parity remains unverified.
- Optional symbolic character status persists in engine saves and maps to script bytes through profile data; unknown legacy state and unsupported status writes fail explicitly.
- Game profiles for Pool of Radiance and Curse of the Azure Bonds (**both unverified**, not playable compatibility claims).

## Build and run

Requires a **C++20 compiler**, **CMake 3.20+**, and **Boost headers 1.75+** (including Boost.JSON).

On Ubuntu/Debian systems supporting Boost.JSON:

```bash
sudo apt-get install cmake ninja-build g++ libboost-dev
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
```

On Windows, install Boost through vcpkg or another supported CMake environment, then configure with your chosen generator and toolchain. Headless builds have no SDL/UI dependencies; enable `GOLDBOX_BUILD_RENDERER` and supply SDL3 >=3.2 for the exploration window.

For WSL builds, use `bash scripts/wsl-build.sh --no-tests=error` after configuring.
The wrapper serializes builds, uses `-j2`, and bounds build/test duration. Put a
wall-clock timeout on interactive or piped binaries; see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

From the repository root, after building:

```bash
./build/apps/goldbox_cli \
  --content examples/content/demo-campaign/journals.json \
  --mods examples/mods --journal 17 --mode enhanced

./build/apps/goldbox_cli \
  --content examples/content/demo-campaign/journals.json \
  --mods examples/mods --journal 17 --mode classic
```

The executable's location varies with the Windows generator; e.g. `build/apps/Debug/goldbox_cli.exe`.

Inspect a user-supplied DOS archive locally without modifying it:

```bash
./build/apps/goldbox_cli --scan-dax /path/to/GEO0.DAX \
  --game-profile games/pool-of-radiance/profile.json
```

For a read-only summary of map records and raw event counts, without printing copyrighted map geometry:

```bash
./build/apps/goldbox_cli --scan-geo /path/to/GEO1.DAX \
  --game-profile games/pool-of-radiance/profile.json

# Only when the exact GEO/ECL record pairing has been verified:
./build/apps/goldbox_cli --scan-geo /path/to/GEO1.DAX --geo-record 20 \
  --ecl-dax /path/to/ECL1.DAX --ecl-record 4
```

The identifiers above are illustrative. Scans do not alter source assets.
With a dispatch profile, explicit GEO/ECL pairing reports resolved move routes
and diagnostics for unresolved routes. Full original-game compatibility has not
been established.

Inventory an installation without writing extracted assets:

```bash
python scripts/scan_installation.py /path/to/POOLRAD --cli build/apps/goldbox_cli \
  --profile games/pool-of-radiance/profile.json > /outside/repository/inventory.json
```

Start the terminal pilot with a verified, explicitly selected map/ECL pair:

```bash
timeout 60 ./build/apps/goldbox_explore games/pool-of-radiance/profile.json \
  /path/to/GEO1.DAX 18 /path/to/ECL1.DAX 18 /outside/repository/state.json
```

Commands are `north`, `east`, `south`, `west`, `search`, `rest`, `init`, `save`,
`load`, and `quit`; menus accept their displayed numeric index. The pilot starts
at `(0,0)` with empty state and does not simulate full campaign initialization.
GEO16 door state 1 permits traversal through a nonzero wall graphic; solid walls,
closed door states 2/3 and map boundaries remain blocking. Door opening/bashing
and map-edge exits are not modeled. Saves
refuse overwrite and reject changed source pairs on load. Choose a fresh save
path for each run and keep saves, reports and captured game text outside this
repository. `timeout` is a WSL/Linux example; native Windows callers must also
bound the process lifetime in their launcher.

### Seeded RNG debug screen

`python scripts/rng_debug.py --engine build/apps/goldbox_rng_probe --image <private-load-image>`
opens a five-minute debug window. Enter a 32-bit seed (decimal or `0x` hex),
runtime bound 0..65535 and 1..64 draws, then choose **Compare rolls**. Each row
shows the original runtime's result and before/after state beside the engine's
C++ result and state. Differences are highlighted. Editing an input clears the
old result. Bound `n` means runtime Random(n), normally 0..n-1; zero still advances
the state. These are runtime bounds, not ECL's inclusive upper operands.

The original side executes locally supplied original routine bytes under the
optional, separately installed Unicorn 2.1.4 analysis tool. Supply
`--unicorn-path <private-python-dependency-directory>` if it is not on Python's
path. `--image` is the existing private 68,592-byte unpacked load image from the
[RNG investigation](docs/research/local-validation-2026-10-15.md#original-dos-random-generator-investigation-2026-10-17),
not START.EXE; its full SHA-256 must match. No original bytes or emulator package
are distributed. Tkinter is required for the window; `--check` instead emits
numeric comparison JSON and exits nonzero on mismatch or failure.

Add `--dosbox <private-reference-directory>/DOSBox.exe` to enable **Capture seed
from private DOSBox**. Use the harness's copied `GAME/POOLRAD/START.EXE` layout,
outside the repository and installed game. Capture launches its own ten-second
reference process, verifies the game fingerprint and relocated resident memory,
then reads the current seed twice without writing process memory. Initial zero
state is skipped; a legitimate all-zero clock seed is therefore inconclusive.
The owned reference is terminated before capture returns. Capture does not
attach to an arbitrary PID or alter an existing game session. Replaying that
seed on both sides remains isolated, not a live trace of the game's next rolls.
With `--dosbox`, the window captures and compares on startup; the capture button
repeats both steps with a fresh reference launch.

The `HighWordLcg32` compatibility primitive accepts caller-supplied multiplier
and increment. Pool's game profile now selects this generator for both character
creation and ECL RANDOM, with one shared stream preserved in engine saves.
The startup seed defaults to 1; `goldbox_explore --seed <decimal-or-0x-uint32>`
overrides it in terminal, window or harness mode. Matching this screen does not
establish complete gameplay/event parity.
Original-code calls have instruction/time budgets and process deadlines; public
CI uses only synthetic inputs and does not require original games or Unicorn.

`goldbox_rng_debug_tests` runs automatically in the existing CTest/CI pipeline.
It checks 280 fixed numeric observations from original runtime execution: five
seeds, seven bounds and eight draws each, including every before/after state.
Expected results are stored as numeric facts, not regenerated from our formula.
Tests also cover continuation, zero-bound consumption, deliberate value/state
mismatches, uninitialized/ambiguous capture, unstable memory reads, timeout and
owned-process/configuration cleanup. No original instructions are in the tests.

The separate `goldbox_rng_original_integration_tests` CTest entry is labelled
`private-assets`. Unconfigured environments explicitly report **Skipped** (exit
77); this is not an original-game parity pass. To run its entire capture/replay
check on native Windows, configure the private inputs and invoke:

```powershell
$env:GOLDBOX_RNG_IMAGE = 'C:\private\pool-load-image.bin'
$env:GOLDBOX_RNG_DOSBOX = 'C:\private\reference\DOSBox.exe'
$env:GOLDBOX_RNG_UNICORN_PATH = 'C:\private\rng-analysis-tools'
python tests/rng_original_integration_test.py build/apps/goldbox_rng_probe
```

The Unicorn path is optional when installed on that Python's normal path. The
test checks 280 original-code/C++ draws, captures a fresh live DOS state, and
checks another 160 draws over five bounds. Values and states must all match.
Partial configuration, bad fingerprints, capture failure, timeouts and mismatch
fail the run. Budgets remain enforced. It needs no manual UI interaction and
does not trace live gameplay draw order.

### Experimental JSONL parity-harness protocol

`goldbox_explore --harness <profile.json> <GEO.DAX> <geo-id> <ECL.DAX> <ecl-id>
<local-save.json>` runs the same exploration session behind a flushed JSONL
protocol instead of the terminal prompt:

- Startup emits a `ready` event with `protocol=1`, the source identity, initial
  position, and `baseline=unverified-empty`.
- Requests use a positive, strictly increasing integer ID, for example
  `{"id":1,"action":"search"}`. Actions are `north`, `east`, `south`, `west`,
  `search`, `rest`, `init`, `save`, `load`, and `quit`. Each line is bounded to
  64 KiB, and CRLF terminators are tolerated.
- VM callbacks surface as `text` and `menu` events; a `menu` expects one
  response such as `{"id":1,"menu_id":1,"choice":0}` with the pending action
  and menu IDs and a zero-based choice. Invalid responses end the session.
- Every accepted action answers with one `complete` event carrying
  `ok`/`blocked`/`unsupported` status, steps and bytecode telemetry, dispatch
  metadata, and the parsed save JSON as `state`; unknown VM failures are
  `unsupported`, never success.
- Protocol violations (malformed JSON, wrong id/action types or values, EOF
  without quitting, overlong lines) emit an `error` event and exit nonzero;
  `quit` completes and exits 0.
- Save/load keep every terminal-pilot safeguard (overwrite refusal, symlink/
  size checks, source-identity mismatch). No controller/emulator integration
  or original-parity claim exists yet; the startup state is an empty,
  unverified baseline. Stdout carries JSONL only, including protocol errors;
  callers must enforce a wall-clock deadline even while a menu awaits input.

Optional: add `--save-meta session.json` to create non-overwriting session metadata. This records only **the startup configuration**, not gameplay state.

### Bounded side-by-side preview controller (experimental, inconclusive)

`python scripts/compare_game.py <session-config.json>` drives **one** engine
harness session (the child engine command already carries `--harness` and its
explicit resource/save arguments) next to **one** reference process, renders
engine events for a human operator, and **never claims parity**: the session is
unpaired/inconclusive by design and no MATCH result is produced.

For code-driven runs, add `--script <scenario.json>`. No LLM or console input is
used. The same controller sends a fixed command sequence, waits for engine
acknowledgments, supplies menu answers, and checks every engine event in order.
It stops at the first mismatch. A scenario for an empty start at row/column zero
with a blocked north move is:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "commands": ["north", "quit"],
  "expect": [
    {"type": "ready", "checks": {"/protocol": 1, "/row": 0, "/column": 0}},
    {"type": "complete", "checks": {"/id": 1, "/status": "blocked", "/row": 0, "/column": 0}},
    {"type": "complete", "checks": {"/id": 2, "/status": "ok"}}
  ]
}
```

Checks use JSON pointers, including array indexes such as
`/state/memory/18944`; values must match exactly, with booleans distinct from
integers. Include text and menu events explicitly. Menu checks can assert
`/choices` and `/menu_id`; the next command supplies a zero-based numeric answer.
Each action event must check `/id`, each completion must check `/status`, and
the script must finish with one `quit` and its successful completion. Missing,
extra or reordered events, invalid choices and unused commands fail the run.
Scenarios are bounded to 256 KiB, 63 commands and 256 expected events. Existing
session deadlines, output limits, ownership, cleanup and private-root locks apply.
Repeated code runs release drained pipe handles, and retain the engine's refusal
to overwrite saves: prepare the same private baseline and a fresh output path.

Success returns zero and prints `[scripted PASS]` only after assertions and
process cleanup succeed. Failure returns nonzero with the event/check that
failed. Python tests can call
`run_session(parse_config(Path('session.json')), ScriptInput(document))` directly
with the `scripts` directory on their module path. `goldbox_scripted_harness_tests`
runs in CTest/CI against the real engine with synthetic map/script resources,
covering repeatability, menus, movement, exact memory, save/load, failure and
deadline paths. Interactive operation remains available without `--script`.

When reference input is configured, scripts can use the existing `reference KEY`
staging, `arm` and `disarm` commands and mirrored action/menu mappings. Rejected
staging/arming commands are fatal in scripted mode. Prepare the reference's known
starting state first; engine acknowledgments do not acknowledge DOS game state.
Scripted PASS verifies engine assertions, **not original-game parity**. This mode
does not inject a DOS seed or control native input-processing timing. Engine
RANDOM and seeded save/reload run in the scripted tests; the original-runtime
comparison remains a separate automated RNG test.

Version-1 session configuration (trusted local execution input; the controller
spawns with `shell=False` and never interpolates shell text; validated fully
before anything is spawned):

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "privateRoot": "C:/outside/the/repository/compare-work",
  "engine": {"command": ["build/apps/goldbox_explore.exe", "--harness",
                         "games/pool-of-radiance/profile.json", "..."],
             "cwd": "C:/abs/engine/dir"},
  "reference": {"command": ["C:/abs/reference/launcher.exe"],
                "cwd": "C:/outside/the/repository/compare-work/reference-copy"},
  "timeoutSeconds": 60,
  "checkpointSeconds": 10
}
```

Operational prerequisites and rules:

- Prepare a **private reference working copy** yourself; the controller never
  copies installed games or edits their config files. Point the reference
  command at that prepared copy and its graphical game/emulator window.
  Keep saves, captures and reports outside the repository. Any
  runnable reference command can still escape its `cwd` on its own; the
  controller does not claim sandboxing of arbitrary reference programs.
- `privateRoot` must be an existing absolute directory outside the repository;
  `reference.cwd` is required inside `privateRoot`. `timeoutSeconds` (default
  60, range 1..600) bounds the whole session; `checkpointSeconds` (default 10,
  positive, at most the total) prints known session state periodically and
  bounds inactivity while waiting for engine startup or an action response.
  Operator/menu input may wait until the total deadline.
- The controller holds an OS-backed single-session lock in `privateRoot`
  (`goldbox-compare.lock`; released on exit, no stale-lock deletion). The lock is
  per `privateRoot` only: two configs with different roots do not exclude each
  other, and engine output paths are not containment-checked. Then it
  launches **both children as fully owned trees**:
  - Windows: a session Job Object with kill-on-close; the child is started
    suspended, assigned to the job, then resumed (no spawn-before-assignment
    escape race). Job Objects support killing every member on close or on
    explicit termination (see
    [Microsoft Job Objects](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/procthread/job-objects)).
  - POSIX: a dedicated session (`setsid`), so the descendant process group is
    killed via `killpg` at cleanup, even when the leader already exited.
    Trusted children must remain in that group; this is not containment for
    programs that deliberately detach into new sessions.
  - Windows callers can select the explicit WSL engine adapter described below.
    Raw `wsl.exe`/`wslg.exe` and the `System32\bash.exe` redirector remain
    rejected as native commands: a Windows Job Object alone cannot own their
    Linux children.
- The operator console renders engine `text`, ordered numbered menu choices,
  position/facing and unsupported diagnostics; raw protocol JSON stays out of
  the normal display. Requests carry strict positive increasing ids; menu
  responses reuse the exact pending action/menu ids. Reference input is manual
  by default. The optional shared-input mode below sends mapped keys only to
  the reference process's owned SDL window.
- Engine `error` events, malformed/out-of-order events, unexpected engine EOF,
  early reference exit, stdout flood (>64 MiB), overlong lines (>8 MiB) and the
  session deadline are all explicit failures that terminate the owned trees;
  controller input waiting never blocks past the deadline. Graceful success
  exists only through an acknowledged `quit`, clean engine exit, drained
  output and verified cleanup. EOF/Ctrl-C/deadline exits fail inconclusively.
  Original-side/reference output is drained
  with hard byte bounds and never rendered or logged.
- Synthetic tests run through the real CLI entry point (and are ctest-bound as
  `goldbox_compare_game_tests`); they cover the valid
  flow and exact id order, malformed configs/protocol, failures, deadline and
  flood, owned-descendant cleanup with an unrelated sentinel surviving, lock
  contention and release, spaced/metacharacter paths with no shell
  interpretation, and an explicit absence of parity-MATCH claims. CTest also
  runs the controller against the compiled engine with synthetic DAX/GEO/ECL
  resources and verifies event state persistence. The controller-only suite
  can run without a build: `python tests/compare_game_test.py`. Research on
  the underlying APIs used [the Python subprocess docs](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/subprocess.html)
  and the Job Objects page above; no third-party code was adopted.

#### Engine inside WSL, reference window on Windows

Run the controller with Windows Python and replace only the `engine` object:

```json
"engine": {
  "backend": "wsl",
  "distribution": "Ubuntu",
  "cwd": "/mnt/c/absolute/path/to/goldbox-engine",
  "command": ["/mnt/c/absolute/path/to/goldbox-engine/build/apps/goldbox_explore",
              "--harness", "games/pool-of-radiance/profile.json",
              "/mnt/c/private/GEO.DAX", "7", "/mnt/c/private/ECL.DAX", "7",
              "/mnt/c/private/state.json"]
}
```

The record IDs above are placeholders for your independently verified local
mapping. `privateRoot`, reference command and reference working directory remain
Windows paths. Engine arguments and `cwd` are Linux paths; no automatic path
translation is attempted. The selected distribution must already have
`/usr/bin/python3` and `/proc`. No systemd user service, installation or network
listener is needed. Existing configurations default to the native backend.

The Linux supervisor relays the unchanged engine JSONL protocol over bounded
pipes. A five-second renewable controller lease and an independent total
deadline stop the session on disconnection or controller failure. Buffered stale
heartbeats cannot extend that lease. An unreaped session anchor reserves the
process-group ID until cleanup; it also kills its group if the supervisor dies.
As with the native POSIX backend, trusted engine children must not deliberately
detach into new sessions. Successful shutdown requires a session-specific
Linux cleanup acknowledgment, drained output and clean launcher exit. A lost
acknowledgment is an explicit failure even when the Linux deadline performs
cleanup. No distribution-wide shutdown or process-name killing is used.

Linux CI runs `goldbox_wsl_supervisor_tests`. On a Windows machine with Ubuntu,
`python tests/wsl_engine_test.py` also checks actual WSL bridging, menu responses,
operator idle lease renewal, controller crashes and unrelated Linux-session
survival. Optionally pass the absolute Linux engine executable and profile paths
as two arguments to include compiled-engine synthetic event/save validation.
These tests launch synthetic children only. The WSL adapter does not establish
parity; original-game input is handled by the separate opt-in mode below.
The implementation uses the Python standard
library and documented [Linux process-group behavior](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/setsid.2.html);
no third-party source was copied or adapted.

#### Shared input for both sides (Windows, SDL 1.2 reference)

Add `input` to the existing `reference` object. Launch the reference DOSBox
executable directly, using a private working copy and configuration that mounts
only that copy. Batch/Steam launchers are not supported for shared input: the
SDL window must belong to the exact launched reference PID.

```json
"input": {
  "backend": "windows-messages",
  "relativeMovement": {
    "forward": ["UP"], "left": ["LEFT"], "right": ["RIGHT"]
  },
  "actions": {"search": ["S"]},
  "menus": {"1": [["Y"], ["N"]]}
}
```

This is a mapping example, not a verified Pool event/menu profile. Supply the
actual original-game hotkeys for each supported action and exact engine menu
ID/choice ordering. Mapping `1` above is usable only for an independently
identified two-choice menu. Missing mappings or mismatched choice counts stop
before either side is dispatched. `save`, `load` and `init` also need explicit
reference mappings; engine saves are not SSI saves. `quit` is controller shutdown
and closes both owned process trees without needing an in-game quit mapping.

The controller launches both sides disarmed. The same stdin command stream can
be written by a person or an LLM driver:

```text
reference ENTER
arm
east
search
1
quit
```

Use `reference KEY ...` only while disarmed to stage the original from observed
screens. Supported keys include letters, digits, arrows, `ENTER`, `ESC`, `SPACE`,
`TAB`, `HOME`, `END`, `BACKSPACE`, and `KP_0`..`KP_9`; sequences are bounded to
16 keys. `arm` asserts that both sides are ready with matching facing; it does
not verify their state. `disarm` returns to staging. Relative movement computes
turns from the last engine facing before sending forward; alternatively, omit
`relativeMovement` and provide explicit absolute direction action mappings.
Unsupported engine actions stop shared input before another action is sent.

Each mapped action or menu response starts engine and reference delivery from
one dispatch gate and waits for both deliveries before accepting the next.
This is concurrent ordered delivery, not atomic execution or a shared emulator
clock. Failure can occur after one side receives input; the controller stops
both sides, reports possible partial delivery, and never retries automatically.
Win32 acknowledgment means the window processed keyboard messages, not that
the original game completed an action or reached an equivalent state. Reference
observation and gameplay parity remain separate work.

The backend forces `SDL_VIDEODRIVER=windib` only for the reference child. It uses
bounded key-down/up messages to exactly one visible `SDL_app` window of that
owned PID, rechecks ownership for each key, and never broadcasts, changes
foreground focus, or injects global keyboard input. Ambiguous or missing windows
fail closed. This is an SDL 1.2 backend, not generic support for SDL 2 or arbitrary
emulators. Research used documented
[Win32 messages](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-sendmessagetimeoutw)
and the upstream [SDL 1.2 message handler](https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL-1.2/blob/main/src/video/windib/SDL_dibevents.c);
no upstream implementation was copied.

`python tests/reference_input_test.py` checks mapping on every platform and,
on Windows, actual message delivery to synthetic reference windows, shared
movement/menu input, disarmed/missing-map rejection, hung-window cancellation,
and an unrelated SDL window receiving no keys. CTest registers the same suite.

#### Verified Steam startup without a manual lookup

Local runtime validation on 2026-10-16 reached the original Pool of Radiance
party menu with Enter and loaded the supplied save into 3D exploration. The
code-wheel screen in this installed build did **not** require looking up an
answer. No original executable or installed configuration was modified.
Community reports of the same behavior were a research lead, not the validation:
[Steam startup discussion](https://steamcommunity.com/app/1882280/discussions/0/3185741160902745033/).

With the reference launched from a private copy, leave shared input disarmed
and send each command only after observing the indicated screen:

1. At the startup/credits screen, send `reference ENTER`. If the wheel prompt
   remains, send Enter at that prompt and verify the party menu before continuing.
2. At the party menu, send `reference L` for Load Saved Game.
3. At the save-slot prompt, send `reference A`. Slot A in the inspected private
   copy loaded a party into 3D exploration at the displayed `(15,4)`, facing west.

The three-command route was repeated through the harness on a fresh private
copy. This is a recipe with observed checkpoints, not a blind startup macro or
a claim that every edition accepts Enter. Save availability and content can
vary. Keep the supplied digital wheel/manuals for editions or in-game content
that need them; do not add proprietary answers or assets to this repository.

Build fingerprints for the local observation (SHA-256):

- `START.EXE`, 65,231 bytes:
  `d825df2b174675c9088ba1489488bdeebe66ad2a22943f17d3a198e60b6a07bd`
- `DOSBox.exe` 0.74-3, 3,745,792 bytes:
  `dcfd46fa521f5ce89dce3bf026056f3a1d15533f80321ee887403e30d7949f5e`

Successful original startup does not establish an equivalent engine baseline.
The prototype engine still starts with independently initialized state; do not
arm shared gameplay merely because the original save has loaded. Map identity,
coordinates, facing, party and event state still need independent alignment.

For character-creation comparisons, the code wheel belongs only to reference
startup. Leave input disarmed, observe and pass the original's startup screens,
and bring each implementation to the same creation checkpoint independently.
Only arm after verifying equivalent selections and state. Never mirror the
wheel's Enter into our engine, add a wheel to its startup, or compensate with
dummy random draws. Edition-specific startup keys belong in reference staging,
not engine rules.

RNG parity additionally needs the original's current generator state at the
common checkpoint, before the first compared draw, and that exact state supplied
to our generator. Equal launch seeds or equal numbers of keypresses are not
evidence of equal state after different startup paths. `arm` neither reads nor
sets either generator. The existing isolated numeric creation tests use explicit
input states; live checkpoint capture and synchronization remain unfinished.
`python tests/reference_input_test.py` regresses staging isolation, unchanged
engine command IDs, and rejection of reference-only keys while armed.

For TypeScript mod SDK authoring (requires Node.js and npm):

```bash
cd packages/mod-sdk
npm install
npm run check
```

## Repository shape

```text
apps/                goldbox_cli and goldbox_explore (terminal pilot, JSONL harness, --window)
engine/include/      Public engine/content/mod interfaces
engine/src/          Core: content/mods, game profiles, ECL VM, exploration, image presentation
```

# Biing! engine and trainer

[Deutsche Anleitung](README.de.md)

A C11/SDL3 reimplementation that reads your own Biing! game files, with a
German/English desktop launcher and a browser trainer for editing live game values.
Supported inputs are the German disk version 1.4 and the German and English GOG
CD editions. No original game files are included.

This is an experimental release. It is playable, but it is not a claim of
complete parity with the original. Read [known differences and support limits](KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md),
especially before moving saves between this engine and the original game.

## Download and play

The [0.1.0-rc.1 release candidate](https://github.com/tstone-1/biing-engine/releases/tag/v0.1.0-rc.1)
includes ready-to-run apps. No Python, compiler or build tools are needed:

- [Windows 11, x86-64](https://github.com/tstone-1/biing-engine/releases/download/v0.1.0-rc.1/Biing-0.1.0-rc.1-windows-x86_64-signed.zip): extract the complete ZIP and open `Biing/Biing.exe`. Signed and timestamped.
- [macOS 27+, Apple silicon](https://github.com/tstone-1/biing-engine/releases/download/v0.1.0-rc.1/Biing-0.1.0-rc.1-macos-arm64-notarized.zip): extract the ZIP and open `Biing.app`. Developer ID signed, notarized and stapled.

Choose **Add game files** or **Add game folder**, import your own copy, then click
**Play**. For the trainer, choose **New trainer session** and **Start trainer**.
Pause before editing values. Your original files stay unchanged and saves live
outside the application.

These are experimental downloads. Windows physical input/focus and first-launch
click-through, trainer browser interaction, and MIDI/CD listening still need manual
acceptance checks. Read the release notes and known limitations before testing.
Checksums, matching source archives and dependency notices are provided.

## Start from source (optional)

Install the prerequisites once:

- **macOS:** install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/), then run `brew install cmake ninja sdl3 uv`.
  Homebrew's setup includes the compiler tools. [SDL3 formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/sdl3).
- **Windows:** install and update [MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org/), open its **CLANG64** terminal,
  and run `pacman -S --needed mingw-w64-clang-x86_64-clang mingw-w64-clang-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-clang-x86_64-ninja mingw-w64-clang-x86_64-sdl3`.
  Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) and reopen the terminal so `uv --version` works.

Download and extract this repository's source ZIP, or clone it. Open a terminal in
that folder (CLANG64 on Windows), then run:

```sh
uv run --no-project python tools/play.py
```

On the first start, paste the path to your disk ZIP, GOG macOS installer/app or
installed game folder when prompted. The script builds the engine and prepares
a separate game copy. Later starts reuse that copy and its saved games. GOG
macOS installers require macOS; an installed game folder works on both systems.
Use `--prepare-only` to build and import without opening the game window.
The game copy and saves live in a `game` folder beside the source folder. Keep that
folder when updating the source. `--game PATH` chooses a different destination.
The project pins Python 3.15.1; uv installs it when needed. The short launcher also
works with an existing Python 3.9+ via `python3 tools/play.py`.

If a build fails, read `build/startup.log` and check the prerequisites above.
An unknown edition is refused. A nonempty destination is kept rather than replaced;
use another `--game` folder to import a different edition.

## Trainer

The desktop launcher has a **Start trainer** button and a session selector. Choose
**New trainer session**, or a dated previous session to continue from its latest
saved/restored checkpoint. Reopening creates a new copy and keeps the previous session.
The **Trainer sessions** button opens their folder. Start the source launcher with
`uv run --no-project python tools/launcher.py` after building; it manages its own
imported-game library, separate from the short source-startup script's `../game` folder.

After building, run:

```sh
uv run tools/biing_inspector.py --game ../game
```

Open the printed local URL beside the game. The trainer uses a separate game copy
under `extracted/inspector-sessions/`; edits and saves stay in that session. Pause
before changing a value. Undo checks the current value before restoring it;
it does not rewind game time. Checkpoints save the game state, not the entire
running process. German and English interfaces are included.
Use your chosen `--game` path if you changed the default. Save a checkpoint before
experimenting; the trainer's game copy is separate from the source launcher's copy.

To recover progress, pause and choose a saved checkpoint, then **Restore checkpoint**.
The trainer first saves the current state as a recovery checkpoint. The restored game
opens at the office (or the bankruptcy screen for negative cash), paused, with the old
undo history cleared. The previous screen and unsaved process caches are not restored.
**Stop session** saves an exit checkpoint. Save a checkpoint before closing the game
window or terminal directly; those exits do not promise an automatic save.
**Open session folder** shows checkpoints (`save-*.sav`), the game copy and edit log.

Reopen a command-line session with:

```sh
uv run tools/biing_inspector.py --resume PATH-TO-SESSION
```

Reopening loads the last saved/restored checkpoint and keeps the session's optional-fix
setting. Without a checkpoint, use the game's Load screen for its retained `GAMES/`
saves. Checkpoints are ordinary edition-specific saves; nothing automatically copies
trainer progress back to your normal game. Keep both copies until you have verified
any manual save transfer. This trainer controls this engine, not the original DOS game.

## Settings and audio

The default preserves original behavior. **Enable optional game bug fixes** in the
launcher, or `tools/play.py --fixes`, enables all switchable corrections. These cover
original UI, calculation, equipment and simulation bugs; they can change game outcomes
and the random sequence. They do not repair every already-damaged save. Hang/crash
guards remain active in either mode. A new CLI trainer accepts `--fixes` too.

For music, close the game and edit only the value after the dash on the `MCARD` line
in the working game copy's `SOUND.CFG`:

| Value | Music |
|---|---|
| `SB`, `SBP`, `SB16` | Sampled game music |
| `CD` | Imported CD tracks, normally used by the GOG editions |
| `GM` | General MIDI through the system synthesizer |
| `ROL` | Roland MT-32 output; requires a matching device or emulator |

The `DCARD` setting controls digital effects/speech. Keep other configuration entries
unchanged. `BIING_MIDI_OUT=list` lists MIDI outputs at engine startup; `none` disables
MIDI output, and a device-name substring chooses an output. General MIDI and MT-32
instrument mappings differ. Native MIDI/CD listening remains a documented test gap.
The launcher offers **Skip intro**; the source startup accepts `--no-intro`.

## Build and test without game files

```sh
cmake -S engine -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build --parallel 4
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
uv run --no-project python -I tools/engine_editions.py --check
uv run --no-project --with pytest python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests
```

The C and included Python tests use synthetic inputs. Some host-dependent checks
can skip when their device is unavailable. They do not test native player input,
speaker output or the original-data import route on a clean computer.

`docs/editions.md` is the editable input for `engine/src/editions_tables.h`.
Run its generator after changing the measurements. Historical references in code
comments may refer to research documents outside this source candidate; they
are not required to compile the engine.

## Desktop packages

Building a package also requires Python 3.15.1 with Tcl/Tk and uv. Build on the target
operating system:

```sh
mkdir -p extracted
git archive --format=zip --prefix=biing-engine/ --output=extracted/project-source.zip HEAD
uv run --no-project --with-requirements packaging/requirements.txt python tools/package_app.py --source-archive extracted/project-source.zip --output extracted/releases/local-test
```

Run these commands from the public source checkout after committing changes. Never
archive a private research repository for distribution. The output directory must not
already exist. Packaging checks the source ZIP against its build inputs and bundles it
with the application. Windows also includes libiconv's corresponding source, downloaded
from its pinned upstream and combined with the included MSYS2 recipe and patches.
`--libiconv-source PATH` can supply the exact reviewed ZIP for an offline build.
Changed runtime binaries require a reviewed update to `packaging/licenses/`.
The recipe expects a Git checkout for its commit/source manifest. Packages bundle the engine, launcher and
runtime, so players need neither a compiler nor Python. Current release-candidate package
checks cover Apple silicon on macOS 27+ and Windows x86-64 on Windows 11. The
default macOS build has an ad-hoc signature. Dependency notices and matching sources
are included. Fresh standard-account import, save/load, update and reinstall retain
saves on both platforms; native UI and audio acceptance remain separate checks.

For Developer ID distribution, `tools/sign_macos.py prepare --app <Biing.app>
--manifest <manifest.json> --output <new-folder>` verifies the packaged files and signs
a copy using `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`. It preserves bundled sources and notices and
requires a secure timestamp and hardened runtime without runtime exceptions.
`tools/sign_macos.py notarize --output <same-folder> --keychain-profile <profile>`
uploads that signed copy to Apple, retains the submission ID for resuming, staples
the accepted ticket and checks Gatekeeper. Keep credentials outside the repository.
Run package acceptance again on the signed artifact. Signing does not publish a release.

On Windows, `tools/sign_windows.py prepare --app <dist/Biing> --manifest <manifest.json>
--output <new-folder> --signer <certificate-common-name>` validates and copies the package
without logging in. `sign --output <same-folder> --ssign <client.exe>
--ssign-sha256 <reviewed-client-sha256>` signs the remaining native files in one batch.
It preserves valid vendor signatures and requires Windows trust verification, timestamps
and the expected signer for new signatures. PowerShell 7 and Windows SDK signtool are
required. Authentication and the pinned client build are described in the tool's docstring;
keep credentials outside the repository and serialize use of a shared signing account.

## License

The project's own code is GPL-3.0-only. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and
[COPYING.txt](COPYING.txt). Original game content is excluded. Third-party
libraries and runtimes retain their own licenses. This is an independent project.

The engine and tools are written from documented formats and measured behavior.
Original graphics, text, music, scene assets and executable files are supplied by
the player at runtime. The source includes functional constants and edition mappings;
these are not a bundled copy of the game. Test media and records are generated
synthetically. The development rules are in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

For a bug report, include your operating system, game edition, source revision and
steps to reproduce it. Include relevant error text, but do not upload original game
files, installers, manuals or extracted game content to an issue.

The intended product keeps its established native disk, hardware, renderer, audio, input, UI, and enhancement owners while executing every remaining 68000 instruction on demand through `shared/amigaport`. The retired offline 68000-to-C product and its generated corpus have been deleted. The adapter now builds against `shared/amigaport`; representative gameplay conformance and hosted release evidence remain open. See `docs/project-state.md` and `docs/migration.md`. No original game disk, Kickstart ROM, WHDLoad file, generated guest code, or reconstructable game asset belongs in the repository or release packages.

These captures document the pre-migration native host and its user-visible features. They are not evidence that the interpreter product is complete. ## Current feature state The canonical inventory is `docs/project-state.md`. In summary: | Capability | State | | --- | --- | | Native pause/options and persistent settings | partial | | Keyboard, controllers, touch, hot-plug, and rebinding | partial | | 60-level selector, progress, locks, and restored difficulty | partial | | Classic/optional platformer physics and interaction reach | partial | | Turbo/Hyper/5x fast-forward with normal-speed audio | partial | | Faithful/native software/Vulkan renderers and effects | partial | | True 16:9, 21:9, and live-window widescreen | partial | | Native disk loading, instant boot, and no floppy waits | partial | | Free camera, cheats, accessibility, savestate diagnostics | partial | | Player save-slot UI and rewind | missing | | `amigaport` maintained 68000 interpreter integration | partial; adapter builds, gameplay evidence remains | | Static translator, generated corpus, and dispatcher removed | verified | | Single-owner native/interpreter gameplay composition | partial; link boundary is in place, runtime audit remains | | Representative cross-host gameplay conformance and performance | missing | | Windows, macOS `.app`, Linux AppImage, Android APK, and WASM Pages releases | verified hosted asset-free matrix; Android publication signing and runtime gates remain open | | Android, browser, and source-launcher disk browse/setup | partial; extensionless disk files and one bounded disk ZIP are accepted, packaged desktop persistence and runtime handoff remain open | | One version identity shown in-game and used for the package and the release tag | verified; `version.txt` is the source, the pause panel shows it, and the publisher refuses a mismatched tag | | Release check with an in-game answer | partial; asks the release service once per launch with the host's own HTTP client and reports a newer release, this build current, or the exact failure — desktop and Android verified, browser run open | ## Player-supplied files The intended product consumes the original three disk images directly. # Speed Haste — Rust port: work log & TODO

A modern Rust port of *Speed Haste* (DOS, 1995, Javier Arévalo / Noriaworks).
Targets: native Linux (SDL3) and web (Dioxus + WebAudio), sharing one core crate.
The registered data blob `SPEEDH.JCL` is **never** shipped; the user provides it.
The shareware release's `SPEEDH.JCL` (freely copyable) is in `shareware/` and
built into the binaries as a fallback (`Jcl::shareware()`).

## Layout

```
crates/core     speedhaste-core   — everything platform independent: data formats,
                                    fixed-point math, game logic, software renderer,
                                    audio mixer + S3M player, GPU scene extraction.
                                    No platform deps.
crates/gpu      speedhaste-gpu    — wgpu renderer for race scenes + frame presentation
                                    (native Vulkan/GL and web WebGL2), texture replacements.
crates/native   speedhaste        — SDL3 frontend (video, audio, keyboard). `speedhaste [PATH/TO/SPEEDH.JCL]`
crates/relay    speedhaste-relay  — WebSocket relay server for network races.
crates/web      speedhaste-web    — Dioxus frontend (file picker, canvas, WebAudio, touch controls).
shareware/      the shareware SPEEDH.JCL, embedded by the core crate.
re/             reverse-engineering scripts, notes, Ghidra/REA config (no game data).
```

## Key design decisions

- **Faithful first.** The core reproduces the original 8-bit software renderer
  (Mode-7 floor, sector walls, scaled RLE sprites, textured/gouraud polygons) into a
  palettized framebuffer, with the same integer/fixed-point maths (wrapping `i32`
  arithmetic, the original sin/cos/atan tables, the same RNG). Physics and AI are
  thus bit-compatible with the original where practical.
  Known quirks kept on purpose (checked in DOSBox): coasting barely slows
  the car — off the gas, `revo` only loses the gear's `accel / 8` per tick
  (no speed-dependent drag; 6th gear's accel is 1/16 of 1st's), so a lap of
  Racer's Edge coasts from 140 to ~110 km/h — and that decay is skipped
  while a Stock car slides (userctl.c), so hard turns can lose less speed
  than going straight.
- **Async game flow.** The original is written as nested blocking loops (menus wait
  for keys, fades spin on VBL). Browsers can't block, so the game flow is ported as
  Rust `async` code: each blocking wait becomes `next_frame().await`. The platform
  polls one future per display frame. This keeps the port structurally close to the
  C source (easy to compare) with no threads/SharedArrayBuffer needed on the web.
- **70 Hz timebase.** The original timer runs at 70 Hz (VGA mode 13h refresh) and
  the race simulates at 70 ticks/s independent of rendering. The core keeps that
  clock; platforms render at whatever refresh rate they have.
- **Upgrade path.** The renderer works on a `Screen` of arbitrary size and the
  original already scales everything by integer `GL_ScreenXRatio/YRatio` (it had a
  640x400 SVGA mode), so higher resolutions come almost for free. Rendering reads
  game state but never mutates it, so an alternative GPU renderer (wgpu/three.js)
  can later consume the same state for filtering/texture replacement. Input is
  DOS scancodes plus platform-neutral gamepad state (`pad.rs`).
- **Gamepads: modern, not faithful.** Pads aim for "plug in an Xbox/DualShock
  pad and play", not the original's calibrated 2-button joystick. Pad *n*
  drives player *n* by default (Setup → Controls can pin a player to
  "Gamepad 1/2", saved as the original's Joystick A/B). In menus the pad
  produces arrow/Enter/Esc key presses; in races it steers through the
  original's analog path (`analog_x`, with the stick's dead zone remapped
  above the game's own ±4) and uses digital controls for the rest, so it
  never presses a keyboard player's keys. Mapping in `pad.rs`'s doc comment.
  Rumble (port addition): crashes into walls/cars and off-road bumping
  queue requests in `World::rumble`; the race maps them to the player's pad
  (SDL3 `set_rumble`, web `vibrationActuator.playEffect`). The controls menu
  drops the original's no-op "Calibrate Joystick" entries.
- **Higher resolutions** (`-scale N`, N > 2): the 3D views render natively at
  320N x 200N (the renderer already scaled by integer ratios). The original's
  HUD layouts only exist for 320 and 640, so above 2x the overlays (HUD,
  countdown, messages) are drawn with the 320 layout on a downsampled copy
  of the frame and only the pixels they change are blown up N x N — crisp
  pixel art, and the translucent minimap stays right (just blocky). Sky and
  unscaled marker sprites are grown by N/2 to keep the 640x400 look. Scale
  1 and 2 are untouched (still pixel-exact).
- **GPU renderer** (`-gpu`, web `?gpu`): when the platform asks
  (`Game::set_gpu`), races and the attract demo hand over a `Scene`
  instead of pixels: `race/render/scene.rs` extracts camera-space
  triangles (walls, billboards, meshes) reusing the software renderer's
  object selection, mesh visibility, lights and face order; the HUD and
  messages are drawn twice on 320x200 (over 0 and over 255) to tell
  opaque, darkened (minimap) and see-through pixels. `crates/gpu` draws
  that with wgpu at the target's resolution:
  - textures stay palettized (R16Uint atlas, 2D array) and are shaded
    through a *lit palette* (palette through each GRAFS.CLR row, rebuilt
    every frame, so VGA fades just work); sky and the Mode-7 floor are
    per-pixel passes using the original's formulas (floor and sky match
    the software pixel for pixel at 320x200);
  - hidden surfaces: walls use true depth, objects their centre depth
    with faces nudged by the software's face order — i.e. the software's
    painter's order between objects (billboards and particles would
    otherwise sink into cars); mesh faces are near-clipped on the CPU at
    the software's plane (4000);
  - translucent faces multiply by the mean luminance ratio of their
    shade row; optional bilinear filtering with smooth shading/fog;
  - only textures + uniforms (no storage buffers), so WebGL2 works. GL
    turns 1-layer textures into plain 2D ones: atlases always get 2+
    layers.
  Menus and software-rendered races are presented by the same renderer,
  so `-gpu` can switch races between renderers at run time (Ctrl+G).
- **Texture replacements** (`-gpu -textures DIR`): PNGs named after the
  game data (IS2 name for sprites/walls, `I3DNAME_n` for mesh material
  n, `GRAFSnnn` floor tiles — turned per map cell — `NUBESn`/`MOUNTn`),
  any size, alpha = holes; `dump_textures` writes the originals with
  those names. True-colour texels can't go through the colour tables,
  so each table row is fitted as an affine colour map (scale + offset per
  channel, least squares over the palette, refit per frame): the
  originals fed back as replacements render within 1.7/255 on average.
- **Network races** (`-relay ws://HOST:8790/ROOM`, web `?relay=...`, then
  Multiplayer Race → Start/Join): `net.rs` ports game/net.c's game side —
  lockstep like the original: everyone simulates the whole race from the
  master's setup and seed, only the humans' per-tick controls travel, a
  tick is simulated once every human's controls for it are known
  (`Player::clock`), and the local player is sampled at most 10 ticks
  ahead of the slowest remote (RACE_HandleComms). The lobby keeps the
  original's steps (SYNC/START, GAMEINFO, NET_SyncStart before each
  race, BYE), up to 4 nodes. IPX and serial/modem are replaced by a tiny
  relay (rooms by URL path; each message goes to the room's others with
  the sender's id) because browsers can only do WebSockets; a reliable
  ordered transport also makes the original's resend logic unnecessary.
  The platform hands the core a `Pipe` of binary messages. Port
  additions: state hashes every 35 ticks ("Out of sync"), "Waiting for
  players", the master's decoration detail for all, and a race ends for
  everyone when a node leaves (the original would hang). Setup →
  Multiplayer (modem phone numbers in the original) shows the server.
- **The software renderer stays.** Even once a GPU (GL/wgpu) renderer exists,
  the faithful 8-bit software renderer remains a first-class, selectable path
  (reference output, low-end fallback, pixel comparisons against the original).
  GPU work goes beside it, never replaces it.
- **Web presentation** uses a plain 2D canvas for the faithful output; with
  `?gpu` the canvas goes to wgpu's WebGL2 backend instead, sized to its
  on-screen size in device pixels. Three.js was dropped in favour of the
  wgpu renderer shared with native (the .wasm grows from 0.8 to 3.6 MB,
  1.4 MB gzipped, mostly wgpu + naga).

## Reverse engineering & REA

The partial original source (https://github.com/TheJare/SpeedHasteSrc) turned out to be
nearly complete for the game itself (it's the later "Circuit Racer" rebrand of the
same code). Missing: the VTAL sound library core (S3M player/mixer), plus small
bits. REA (Reverse Engineer Anything, https://github.com/morluto/rea) is used to
check the shipped `SPEED.EXE` against the source and to recover what's missing.

### Getting REA to analyze a DOS/4GW binary

1. `SPEED.EXE` is an MZ stub + **LE** (linear executable) for DOS/4GW. REA's Ghidra
   adapter explicitly rejects LE/LX (it supports MZ, COM, raw, ELF, PE, ...).
   REA's raw-binary mode maps file offset 0 at the entry point, which doesn't fit a
   two-object LE image either.
2. Solution: `re/scripts/le2elf.py` parses the LE object/page tables, applies all
   internal fixups (9259 32-bit offset fixups + 1 selector) and writes a static
   i386 ELF with both objects at their preferred bases (code 0x10000, data 0x60000).
   Ghidra (through REA) loads it as a normal ELF: 739 functions, 670 strings.
3. Ghidra has no Watcom compiler spec. Watcom's register convention (args in
   EAX, EDX, EBX, ECX; callee saves everything) is added via
   `re/ghidra-watcom/x86watcom.cspec` + `install.sh`, selected with
   `REA_GHIDRA_COMPILER_SPEC_ID=watcom` (REA validated and accepted the custom id).
4. The REA CLI starts a fresh Ghidra import per command (~22 s each). To keep one
   analyzed session alive, `re/scripts/rea_daemon.py` runs `rea --mcp` (stdio MCP)
   and exposes it on a Unix socket; `re/scripts/reaq.py TOOL '{json}'` sends single
   tool calls (open_binary, search_strings, xrefs, procedure_pseudo_code, ...) and
   prints the `normalized_result`. After the first query, calls take ~30 ms.

```sh
. re/rea-env.sh
python3 -I re/scripts/le2elf.py refs/full-game-dos/SPEED.EXE re/out/speed.elf
python3 -I re/scripts/rea_daemon.py $PWD/re/out/rea.sock &
python3 -I re/scripts/reaq.py open_binary '{"path":"'$PWD'/re/out/speed.elf","provider_id":"ghidra"}'
python3 -I re/scripts/reaq.py search_strings '{"pattern":"create player"}'
python3 -I re/scripts/reaq.py procedure_pseudo_code '{"procedure":"0x3d2b8"}'
```

First result: string "Can't create player" → xref 0x3d446 → `FUN_0003d2b8`, which
decompiles to an exact match of `THN_AddThing()` in `things.c`.

REA friction worth noting: LE unsupported (wrote le2elf.py), no Watcom cspec
(added one), ~22 s CLI round trips (wrote the MCP socket daemon), decompiler
names register args `unaff_*` because of the callee-saves-all convention, and
string search results sometimes include stray leading bytes — and occasionally
miss a string entirely when Ghidra merged it into a preceding one ("Mr. Shy" is
in the binary but `search_strings` didn't find it; a raw byte dump did).

## Data formats (all inside SPEEDH.JCL)

- **JCL**: archive; trailer at EOF-16: magic `0xdf73b489`, nfiles, realnfiles,
  dirsize. Directory of 32-byte entries (name[24], offset-from-dir-start (backwards), size).
- **PAL**: 768 bytes, 6-bit VGA RGB. **PIX**: raw 320-wide 8-bit images.
- **CLR**: colormaps, 32 levels x 256 (light/fog translation tables).
- **GRAFS.DAT**: 252 floor tiles of 64x64.
- **MAPxx.DAT**: 2+2 byte header, 64x64 u16 tile indices, 64x64 u8 rotations, then
  (x,y,angle,type) u16 thing records. **.SEC**: text sector map. **.PTH**: AI path.
- **IS2**: RLE sprite (column- or row-major), 24-byte header.
- **I3D**: "B3D" binary dump of Watcom `O3DM_TObject` (pointers as offsets), then textures.
- **FNT**: fonts. **RAW**: 8-bit unsigned PCM. **S3M**: Scream Tracker 3 music.

## Work log

- **Session 1**: Explored refs. Set up git, REA + Ghidra 12.1.4 + JDK 21,
  LE→ELF converter, Watcom cspec, REA MCP daemon. Read most of the game source.
  Core crate: data formats, fixed-point maths, async runtime, SDL3 frontend.
  Ported the race end to end (renderer, physics, AI, HUD), S3M player (checked
  vs libopenmpt), the whole front end (intro, menus, records, credits, demo),
  and the Dioxus web frontend (tested in headless Chromium). DOSBox reference
  harness: main menus pixel-identical. REA used to find shipped-vs-source
  differences (intro sequence, logo table) and to verify polygon code.
- **Session 2**: Fixed texture garbling on cars (tail lights when turning,
  rims, decals; reported from play testing). Cause: the texture fillers pack
  (tx, ty) as `SHL EBP,8` + `MOV BP,WORD PTR [tx+1]`. The `MOV` *replaces*
  the low word, but the port OR-ed it in, so ty's low fraction bits leaked
  into tx's integer bits. With `pack()` masking the high word, the car-select
  small cars now match DOSBox **pixel for pixel** (was ~90 differing pixels),
  which also validates the polygon filler used in races.
  GamePal colours 0-15/240-255 (placeholders in grafs.pal) come from the DAC
  after LLS_Init's BIOS mode set, i.e. the **VGA BIOS default palette**, with
  or without `-nologo`; the port had zeroed them. Found by mapping the
  course-select diff to palette indices (15 → white, 246/247 → dark grey),
  then matching against DOSBox's built-in table. REA read the shipped VGA
  fade routines (missing from the source); the full fade towards RGB uses
  64 - pos, not 65 - pos. Course select now differs only in the record time.
  Gamepad support (SDL3 gamepads, web Gamepad API standard mapping). REA
  showed the shipped `UCT_GetUserControl` (0x405e4) and `UpdateJoystick`
  (0x24f90); per the user, the pad design favours modern ergonomics over
  the joystick model. Tested headless (`pad:` script step), with an SDL
  virtual gamepad, and in Chromium with a stubbed `getGamepads()`.
  Web: SPEEDH.JCL is remembered in IndexedDB (Play / Forget it on the
  loader). Audio goes through an AudioWorklet: the mixer stays on the main
  thread (no SharedArrayBuffer/COOP needed), the frame loop keeps ~80 ms
  queued, the worklet reports frames played; ScriptProcessorNode remains as
  the fallback where AudioWorklet is missing (non-secure contexts).
  Ported the hidden greetings starfield (hold I+G+N in the main menu); REA
  confirmed it ships. The original reads one past its 1/z table for stars
  at exactly ZMAX; the port extends the table instead.
  RNG order in the off-road dust spawn: read the shipped code with objdump
  (Ghidra hadn't split those functions out); y's offset is drawn first.
  Tip: `objdump -d -M intel re/out/speed.elf` + grep for the inlined RNG
  (`add eax,0xb35fa137`) finds every random draw quickly.
  VTAL music: read the S3M loader/player with REA and recorded the original
  in DOSBox (SB Pro, `re/scripts/dosbox_audio.sh`). The player now does what
  VTAL does: every song hard-panned by channel setting (MENUS, SCIRCUIT,
  HASTE5/8 were mono before), PanWidth applied as /256, master/global volume
  ignored (HASTE2 and FIN were half volume), fast volume slides, tone porta
  and vibrato on tick 0, volume ≤ 63. Against the capture our L/R balance
  now correlates (0.41, was 0) and the side/mid ratio matches. HASTE9: ours
  and libopenmpt match the original equally (~0.70, the 8-bit capture's
  ceiling), so its lower libopenmpt score wasn't a port bug.
- **Race is pixel-exact vs the original.** Ran the original under `faketime`
  (fixed BIOS clock → fixed RND seed), drove it into a single race, captured
  frames, then brute-forced our `-seed` (= the original's BIOS_Clock at
  init, here 1129) with the `race_seed` example. Two fixes got every frame
  to 0 differing pixels: the column drawer is now a register-faithful port
  of vertdrwa.asm walking the IS2 RLE data (its transparent-run skips round
  up and the fraction's low word doubles as the pixel counter, so it samples
  differently from plain stepping — visible in the speckled grandstand
  textures and scaled sprites); and the remaining "differences" were DOSBox
  screenshot tearing (rows 0-99 of tick t over rows 100-199 of tick t+2).
  So physics, AI, RNG use, cameras, HUD and the renderer all match over
  11 s of racing with 19 AI cars.
  Music/effects balance: recorded the original's race with music muted
  (MusicVolume 0) and compared effect levels with ours on the same seed:
  ours were 0.68 of the original vs 0.45 for music, so the music level went
  up 1.5×. Found on the way: the original ignores `MusicOn No` once the
  first song starts (MENU_InitMusic always applies MusicVolume); the port
  keeps honouring MusicOn (deliberate deviation; the game's menus can't
  change it anyway). Headless gained `audio:PATH` and `HEADLESS_CFG`.
- **Session 3**: GPU renderer, end to end. Core: races and the demo build
  `Scene`s when asked (overlays classified by drawing them twice), F12 is
  off under the GPU (it composes at 320x200). Found while checking the
  scene maths: the projection is `focus/16` for walls, meshes and floor
  alike (sprites used `focus`), now `SceneView::focus`. New `crates/gpu`
  (wgpu 30): first headless comparison already matched the software
  layout; floor/sky pixel-identical, remaining differences are texture
  sampling details (perspective-correct vs the original's affine fillers
  and RLE column stepping). Dust particles disappeared into the cars with
  a plain z-buffer → objects now sort by centre depth like the software's
  painter. Filtering showed seams from wrapping (sky top, wall tops,
  sprite edges) → per-axis clamp flags. Native: wgpu surface on the SDL
  window (wgpu 30 wants the display handle on the instance; SDL's Window
  isn't Send, so its raw handle is wrapped), tested under Xvfb +
  lavapipe with xdotool. Web: WebGL2 backend, tested in headless
  Chromium; textures were black at first (1-layer array → GL 2D
  texture). Texture replacements with an affine fit of the colour table
  rows for lighting/fog, round-trip checked with the dumped originals,
  and with 4x-upscaled ones. No REA work this session: the GPU path
  builds on the already-verified software renderer.
  Network play (the last TODO item, first marked "not planned"): the
  released game/net.c and race.c's RACE_HandleComms were complete enough
  to port the protocol (no REA needed). The first two-node test desynced
  as soon as the cars moved: remote players had no key bindings, and gear
  changes compare the tick's scancode with the player's keys — which is
  why the original's SYNC packet carries everyone's keys. Then a stale
  hash from the end of race 1 failed a check in race 2 of a championship
  → messages carry the race number. Verified: 3 in-process nodes with
  100 ms latency (306 checks, 0 failed), championship continuation,
  leaving mid-race, two native windows through the real relay, and a
  native host racing a Chromium client in lockstep (x86-64 vs wasm32
  identical).
- **Session 4**: Shareware and touch. The shareware SPEEDH.JCL is the
  registered one minus circuits 3-8 (map02-07 .dat/.pth/.sec), with its
  own SPHLOGO.PIX and an ENDTEXT.BIN (the 80x25 text screen fl2.c copies
  to video memory on exit). The menus had already
  ported every GL_Registered check but the flag was hardcoded true; now it
  is `Data::is_registered()` (map07.sec present, as fl2.c). Headless runs
  confirmed the original's shareware behaviour: Championship shows
  "REGISTERED VERSION ONLY", circuits 3+ and cars 2+ blink "Registered
  Version" and refuse Enter, the demo races circuit 1. The JCL is
  `include_bytes!`'d in core and borrowed (`Jcl` holds `Cow<'static,
  [u8]>`), so no 6 MB copy at startup; the web wasm grows to 9.7 MB
  (4 MB gzipped). Native falls back to it with no path and no
  ./SPEEDH.JCL; the web start page has "Play Shareware Version".
  Touch controls (web only), after the stunt-car project's overlay: a
  virtual gamepad merged into pad 1 (`touch.rs`), so races and menus
  needed no changes beyond `Game::in_race()` to switch layouts. Sized
  for the black bars beside the 4:3 picture on a phone held sideways;
  upright, the picture moves to the top. Name entry gets the phone's
  keyboard through a hidden text field (kept holding one space so
  Backspace on an empty field still fires an input event). Tested in
  headless Chromium with CDP multi-touch (steer + gas held together) in
  both orientations; not yet on a real phone.
  Phone vibration, dropped again: the touch controls first passed the
  race's rumble requests (wall and car hits, strong motor only) to
  `navigator.vibrate(ms)`. Firefox for Android crashed on every wall hit
  with it — the whole browser, which a page shouldn't be able to do — and
  was fine with it switched off (user-tested). Not a call-rate problem:
  headless Chromium counted ~7 calls in 6 s of wall crashes. Could come
  back later, e.g. off by default or not on Firefox for Android; the
  rumble requests are still there (`Game::take_rumble(0)`) for gamepads.
  GAS and BRAKE became one pedal (gas in the top 65%, brake below,
  following the finger) after user feedback: the game barely slows off
  the gas (a kept quirk, see design decisions), so on a phone the brake
  must be one thumb-rock away rather than a lift and re-press.
  Exit text screen (`textscr.rs`): the shareware's ENDTEXT.BIN holds
  leftovers of an older text drawn green on green (attribute 0x22), so
  it has to be shown with its attributes; hidden cells become spaces.
  Without the file (registered data) fl2.c's DrawBar fills the top line
  with "SPEED HASTE v1.00" in 0x2E — that string is in the shipped
  SPEED.EXE next to "endtext.bin", but the bar itself wasn't compared
  with DOSBox. Native prints it on exit in 24-bit ANSI colour (plain
  text when stdout isn't a terminal); checked in xterm. The web page
  shows it as coloured monospace text in place of the canvas, with
  "Play again". Note the shareware's Quit first shows its graphical nag
  screen (the shareware SPHLOGO.PIX), which waits for a key.

## Building & running

```sh
# Native (needs libsdl3-dev): config/records go to $XDG_DATA_HOME/speedhaste
cargo run --release -p speedhaste -- /path/to/SPEEDH.JCL [-nologo] [-track N -car N]
# Without a path: ./SPEEDH.JCL, else the built-in shareware version.

# Web (needs `cargo install dioxus-cli`): serve the output dir, open, pick SPEEDH.JCL
dx build --package speedhaste-web --platform web --release   # run from the workspace root
python3 -m http.server -d target/dx/speedhaste-web/release/web/public 8765
# URL query = original options, e.g. http://localhost:8765/?nologo&track=3
# Touch controls: on where the primary pointer is a finger; ?touch=1 / ?touch=0
# or the start page's toggle (saved in localStorage) override.
# Higher race resolution (port addition): -scale N (web: ?scale=N) makes the
# SVGA setting / F12 use 320N x 200N instead of 640x400 (N = 2..8).
# GPU renderer (port addition): -gpu (web: ?gpu) draws races with wgpu at the
# window's resolution; Ctrl+G switches races GPU <-> software, Ctrl+F toggles
# filtering (-filter / ?filter to start with it). Native -textures DIR loads
# replacement PNGs (write the originals with the dump_textures example).
cargo run --release -p speedhaste -- SPEEDH.JCL -gpu -filter -textures DIR
# Network races: run a relay somewhere reachable, then every player starts
# the game with the same room URL and picks Multiplayer Race (one Starts,
# the others Join; -master / -slave skip that menu). Web: ?relay=URL (a page
# served over https needs a wss:// relay, e.g. behind a TLS proxy).
cargo run --release -p speedhaste-relay -- 0.0.0.0:8790
cargo run --release -p speedhaste -- SPEEDH.JCL -relay ws://HOST:8790/myroom
```

## Testing helpers

- `cargo run -p speedhaste-core --example headless -- SPEEDH.JCL SCRIPT OUTDIR [game args]`
  runs the game without a window at simulated 60 fps with scripted keys
  (`wait:N`, `key:NAME`, `down:NAME`, `up:NAME`, `shot:NAME`, `raw:NAME`,
  `pad:lx=-1/rt=1/SOUTH`), saving PPMs.
  Game args like `-track 3 -car 2` jump straight into a race.
- `cargo run -p speedhaste-core --example dump -- SPEEDH.JCL OUTDIR [meshes]` dumps assets.
- `re/scripts/web_test.mjs` drives the web build in headless Chromium (Playwright):
  loads SPEEDH.JCL through the file input, scripted keys and a fake gamepad (`pad:SPEC`),
  canvas screenshots.
- `re/scripts/web_touch_test.mjs` drives the touch controls on a phone-sized
  touch viewport (`VIEWPORT=390x844` for upright) with the built-in
  shareware: `tap:SELECTOR`, `hold:`/`release:SELECTOR`, `steer:DX` /
  `steer:off`, `click:TEXT`, `type:TEXT`, `shot:NAME`. Playwright's own
  browser isn't installed here; scripts use `/usr/bin/chromium`
  (`executablePath`, env `CHROMIUM`). Race from the menu:
  `tap:.t-enter,wait:1500,tap:.t-down,wait:300,tap:.t-enter,wait:3500,tap:.t-enter,wait:4000,tap:.t-enter`.
- `re/scripts/web_audio_check.mjs` checks the web audio output (AudioWorklet
  chunk pacing and loudness).
- `re/scripts/dosbox_audio.sh OUT.raw SECONDS -nologo` records the original's
  audio (SB Pro through VTAL's mixer); `re/scripts/cmp_capture.py` compares it
  with `cargo run --release -p speedhaste-core --example s3m_render -- SPEEDH.JCL
  SONG.S3M 22050 SECONDS PANWIDTH OUT.raw` renders.
- Pixel-exact race check: `faketime -f '@2026-01-01 00:01:00' dosbox -conf
  re/dos/dosbox_nl.conf` (the usual conf with `speed.exe -nologo`), then
  `dosbox.sh key Return; key Down Return; key Return; key Return` and `shot`s
  during the race; `race_seed SPEEDH.JCL SHOT.ppm FROM TO MAXTICKS` (release
  example) finds the seed and tick that match (BIOS_Clock ≈ 18.2 × seconds
  since midnight + boot ticks). Env `RACE_SEED_DUMP=1` saves the best frame,
  `RACE_SEED_SAVE_TICK=N` a given tick. Beware screenshot tearing.
- `re/scripts/cmp_audio.py` compares our S3M renders with libopenmpt's.
- `cargo run --release -p speedhaste-gpu --example gpu_shot -- SPEEDH.JCL OUTDIR
  FRAMES WxH [game args]` runs the game twice headless (software and GPU
  races, same args) and saves `soft_N.ppm` / `gpu_N.ppm` (GPU at WxH, on
  lavapipe here). Env `KEYS=N:NAME,...` taps keys at frames (into a single
  race: `KEYS=31:ESC,333:ENTER,365:DARROW,367:ENTER,619:ENTER,921:ENTER`,
  shots from ~1300), `GPU_FILTER=1`, `TEXTURES=DIR`. Audio is mixed each
  frame because menus wait for music fades.
- `cargo run --release -p speedhaste-gpu --example dump_textures -- SPEEDH.JCL
  OUTDIR` writes every replaceable texture as a PNG.
- `cargo run --release -p speedhaste-core --example net_test -- SPEEDH.JCL OUTDIR
  FRAMES SCRIPT_A SCRIPT_B [...]` plays a network race between several games
  in one process (in-memory relay, env `NET_DELAY=frames` latency) and prints
  the desync checks. Scripts: `N:KEY` tap, `N:+KEY`/`N:-KEY` hold/release,
  `N:shot:NAME`. Master into a single race / slave joining:
  `31:ESC,333:DARROW,335:ENTER,365:ENTER,395:DARROW,397:ENTER,619:ENTER,760:ENTER,1000:ENTER`
  and `31:ESC,333:DARROW,335:ENTER,365:DARROW,367:ENTER,1000:ENTER`.
- Native network runs print the checks with `SPEEDHASTE_NET_DEBUG=1`. Two
  native windows under Xvfb + a Chromium page can share one relay (see the
  session 3 log); in Playwright scripts leave ~300 ms between keys, or two
  taps land in the same frame.
- `re/scripts/dosbox.sh start|key|down|up|shot NAME|stop` drives the *original*
  game in DOSBox under Xvfb (`Xvfb :99`) and grabs 320x200 reference frames
  into `re/dos/capture/` (the game is copied to the gitignored `re/dos/game`).

# Provenance and licensing boundary

Pinball Fantasies Native is a source-guided native reimplementation. The public repository contains the project-authored Go implementation, build tooling, tests and documentation. It does not contain the original commercial game payload.

## Historical reference

Development consulted the historical source repository:

- upstream: `https://github.com/historicalsource/pinballfantasies`
- pinned reference commit: `aa2dd368d73886bbd666507bd7341001060700d9`

That historical source is not bundled in this repository or in release binaries. No open-source license was identified in the pinned historical tree, so this project does not purport to relicense it.

## Original game data

Users provide their own legally obtained DOS copy of Pinball Fantasies. PRG, MOD, legacy HI, configuration, artwork, music and other original commercial data remain outside the project license.

The public release artifacts are asset-free. Original game files are read as data containers and their x86 code is never executed.

## Project license

The native implementation and project-authored material are released under the MIT License, copyright (c) 2026 voobrazimoe.

The MIT license applies only to material for which this project can grant those terms. It does not grant rights to Pinball Fantasies itself, its original commercial data, artwork, music, trademarks or historical/reference source material.

## Public history

The public repository was created from an audited source snapshot with fresh Git history rather than by exposing the private development history. Local personal builds that embed commercial inputs are kept outside the public repository and are not project release artifacts.

# Changelog

## 0.1.0 (2026-10-18)

The first release: a port of the whole game for Windows x64. You need your own copy of the original
game files (see README.md, How to play).

### The game

- The whole original chain runs as it did: SETUP, the MicroProse logo, the intro, the shell (pilot roster,
  options, orders, the briefing map, arming and launch), the missions in all theatres, and the debrief
  (landing, eject or rescue, crash, medals, promotion, the roster).
- AdLib sound: the logo, the intro and shell music, the flight sounds and the debrief music, through the
  Nuked-OPL3 emulator.
- The error log `f117.log` beside the program records each error the game reports, with its date.
- Fixed: Esc no longer quits the whole game when a program ends (a crash into the sea returned to the desktop).

### The launcher (`F-117A Nighthawk.exe`)

- Pick the game folder, the program, the aspect (4:3 or 1:1), the window size and full screen, and whether
  sound is on. Play starts the game; the launcher stays open. All of it is remembered in `settings.ini`.
- **Game speed** (default 7, about 10 frames a second): the original paces itself to about 17 frames a second
  on today's PCs, which spins the radar dishes far too fast. 0 gives back the original pacing.
- **Key Bindings...**: all 56 actions on four tabs, with Reset to defaults. Changed keys are saved and
  passed to the game with `--keys`.

### Command line

- `--frame-ticks N`: the game speed for `f117.exe` itself (the launcher passes its value).
- `--keys NAME=CODE,...`: the key bindings for `f117.exe`.
- `--version` prints the version. `--check` checks the game folder.

### How it was verified

- Every module was compared with the original code under emulation (Unicorn), byte for byte: the
  program loader, the video driver, the sim flow, the flight and weapons code, the 3D renderer, the
  shell, the front end, the debrief and the sound driver.
- 23 automated tests (`ctest`) run the chain of programs and the checks against the original. The tests
  that need the game files skip themselves when they are not there.

### Known issues

- Low over the sea near the left edge of the screen, a possible land strip can show. It is not investigated yet.
- Speech is silent. The Roland, PC speaker and IBM/Tandy sound choices play as AdLib; the Sound Blaster and
  Pro Audio Spectrum digital sound states are not ported.
- The mouse and the joystick are untested in the shell and the debrief.
- The radar dish spin depends on the game speed (0 = the original pacing).
- The ID quiz is not present: it is dead code in this version of the original.

### Playtested

The whole game was played through in this port and checked by the user (2026-10-18/19): the front end, the shell,
missions with combat, crashes and ejection, the cockpit, the 3D view, the sound, the debrief, the game speed and
the key bindings.

# Known differences and support limits

This experimental engine supports the German disk version 1.4 and the German and
English GOG CD editions. It identifies those builds and refuses unknown versions.
It needs the player's own files; no game or manual download is provided.

## Differences from the original

| Area | What differs |
|---|---|
| Random simulation | The generator uses measured inputs, but individual games do not follow the original's exact random sequence. Statistics and individual actions have been compared; identical outcomes are not promised. |
| Original bugs | Most original behavior, including bugs, is retained by default. `tools/play.py --fixes` enables optional corrections. Guards against hangs, crashes and invalid memory accesses are always active. |
| Manual query and saves | The original's manual question and related rewards/penalties are not implemented. Save files retain associated counters using the disk-edition rule on all editions. Loading an engine save in the original can activate penalties until its manual question is answered. Keep backups and use the same game edition when transferring saves. |
| Extra programs | The external miniature-golf game, its handover, DOS setup/helper programs and the shooter are not implemented. Existing configuration files and defaults supply settings. |
| Intro and DOS behavior | DOS text-mode moments appear black. Hardware setup, DOS error paths and some transition details are not reproduced; CD audio timing has a small lead-in difference. |
| Timing and pointer | The main loop runs at a fixed 50 Hz. Machine-speed-dependent ambience, intro fast-forward and stalls can differ. Mouse movement follows the host pointer rather than DOS relative-motion behavior. |
| Invalid or unsaved original state | Some rare newspaper wording, pathology and torture behavior depends on original memory outside saved records. The engine uses defined fallbacks. An unreachable large one-shot sound-driver bug is also not reproduced. |

## What has been verified

Automated checks cover synthetic formats, game rules, input adapters, audio-buffer
handling, save operations, the launcher and trainer protocol. Separate local checks
using owned game files cover import and engine output for all three editions on
macOS, and disk-edition import on Windows. The source CI runs on macOS and Windows
without original game files.

The current native build environments are Apple silicon/macOS 27 and Windows 11
x86-64. A macOS disk-edition manual smoke test covered mouse, keyboard, focus return
and digital audio. Native Windows input/focus and MIDI/CD listening have not received
the same acceptance check. Automated audio checks do not establish speaker output.
Older macOS, Intel Macs and Linux are not claimed as tested platforms.

The trainer's German/English labels, named records, validated editing, undo,
checkpoint restore and session reopening have automated coverage. A complete native browser layout/reconnect
acceptance run remains open. Undo reverses one validated field edit; it does not
rewind time or all consequences of that edit.

## Downloads and support

The [0.1.0-rc.1 prerelease](https://github.com/tstone-1/biing-engine/releases/tag/v0.1.0-rc.1)
provides signed Windows 11 x86-64 and notarized macOS 27+ Apple silicon apps, with
dependency notices and matching source archives. Fresh standard-account import,
save/load, update and reinstall preserve saves on both platforms. Native UI and audio
acceptance remain incomplete as described above; these are experimental packages.
The packaging recipe's default macOS build is only ad-hoc signed. Notarization applies
to the explicitly labelled published archive, not every locally built test ZIP.

Back up saves before testing a new version or using the trainer. Report reproducible
problems through this repository's issues with edition, platform and revision.
Original game files and extracted media must stay out of issues and contributions.
